Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in France. Prescription-only (Liste I or II). EU/EEA travelers need Schengen certificate. Non-EU travelers should carry doctor's letter translated into French. Max 3 months' personal supply.

Adderall / amphetamines is restricted in France. Amphetamines are stupéfiants (narcotics). Adderall is not approved in France; methylphenidate is the standard ADHD treatment. Travelers must have Schengen certificate (EU) or certified medical attestation (non-EU). Very strict enforcement.

Cannabis / CBD is banned in France. France has some of the strictest cannabis laws in Western Europe. Recreational use is illegal; a 2020 reform introduced a €200 flat fine for simple possession. Medical cannabis pilot program began 2021 but remains very limited. CBD products with 0% THC were legalized after EU court ruling. Do not import any cannabis products.

Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is restricted in France. Classified as a stupéfiant (narcotic). Requires special prescription (ordonnance sécurisée) in France. Travelers need Schengen certificate (EU) or certified attestation. Maximum 30 days' supply.

Codeine / opioids is restricted in France. Codeine was reclassified to prescription-only in 2017 (previously OTC in some combinations). Stronger opioids are stupéfiants with 28-day maximum prescriptions. Carry all documentation.

Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is caution in France. Available OTC in pharmacies but pharmacist must verify no contraindications. No special import restrictions for personal quantities. Limited to small pack sizes per purchase.
Psilocybin / MDMA is banned in France. Both are stupéfiants (narcotics). Possession is a criminal offense carrying up to 1 year imprisonment and €3,750 fine. No approved medical use programs.
Tramadol is restricted in France. Prescription-only (Liste I) since tighter controls were introduced. Not classified as a stupéfiant but requires ordonnance. Carry prescription for travel.
Tranquilizers / sleeping pills (zolpidem) is restricted in France. Prescription-only medication (Liste I). Standard documentation required. Available at French pharmacies with local prescription.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — The Lake Annecy Promenade Distraction (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Pickpockets work the crowds around Lake Annecy, the Palais de l’Ile, and the Old Town, usually in pairs or small teams. One person uses a distraction — asking for directions, staging a photo — while the other lifts wallets and phones. The lakefront promenade during the summer months sees the most incidents. How to avoid: Use a cross-body bag with zipped compartments. Keep valuables in front pockets or inside jacket pockets. Stay alert in crowded areas. Never leave bags on chairs or the ground in restaurants.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — Beach Belongings Theft (theft, severity: moderate). Thieves patrol the lakeshore beaches watching for swimmers who have left bags unattended on towels. They wait until you’re in the water or turned away, then scoop up wallet, phone, and keys and disappear into the crowd. Incidents spike during July and August at the busier beaches. How to avoid: Never bring valuables to the beach. Leave jewelry and passports at your hotel. Use a waterproof pouch for essentials. Take turns swimming with companions so someone watches belongings.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — Dual Menu Restaurant Scam (tourist-trap, severity: low). Some restaurants in tourist areas maintain two sets of menus — one for locals with standard prices and another for tourists with inflated prices. Additionally, menus may lack prices entirely, only revealing exorbitant costs when the bill arrives. Hidden charges for bread, water, or cover fees may appear. How to avoid: French law requires restaurants to display menus with prices outside. Ask for a menu with prices before ordering. Walk away from restaurants without posted prices. Verify the bill matches menu prices.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — Fake Petition and Charity Clipboard Scam (distraction, severity: moderate). Scammers approach tourists in the Old Town with clipboards asking for signatures on a petition for a charitable cause. After you sign, they demand a donation of €10–€20. The clipboard keeps your hands and eyes occupied while an accomplice works your bag from behind. The petitions feature photocopied logos from legitimate French charities — but the operation is entirely fraudulent. How to avoid: Never stop for anyone with a clipboard. Say ‘Non merci’ firmly and keep walking. Keep hands on your belongings if approached. Legitimate charities do not solicit on streets with petitions.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — The Gold Ring Trick (distraction, severity: low). A scammer ‘finds’ a gold ring on the ground near a tourist and asks if they dropped it. When the tourist says no, the scammer offers to sell it as a ‘lucky find’ for a significant sum, claiming it is valuable gold. The ring is worthless metal. This scam, common in Paris, occasionally appears in smaller French tourist towns. How to avoid: Never engage with anyone claiming to find valuables near you. Say ‘Non’ and walk away immediately. Do not touch or examine anything offered.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — Friendship Bracelet Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: low). Scammers aggressively approach tourists and begin tying a ‘friendship bracelet’ onto their wrist without permission. Once the bracelet is tied, they demand payment, often 10-20 euros or more, becoming aggressive if refused. While attempting to remove the bracelet, accomplices may pickpocket the distracted victim. How to avoid: Keep your hands in pockets or crossed when walking. Never let strangers touch your hands or wrists. Walk away immediately saying ‘Non merci’ firmly.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — Rental Car Break-ins (theft, severity: high). Thieves target rental cars, easy to pick out by their license plates, missing floor mats, and sterile interiors. They smash windows to pull out luggage, electronics, and valuables, sometimes dropping the rear seats to get at the trunk. Parking at trailheads and scenic viewpoints above the lake is where most break-ins happen — exactly where you’ll want to stop on a day trip. How to avoid: Never leave any valuables visible in your car. Remove all items including charging cables. Use staffed parking lots when available. Consider sedan rentals with proper trunks rather than hatchbacks.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — Vacation Rental Fraud (online-fraud, severity: high). Scammers create fake vacation rental listings for properties in Annecy that either do not exist or belong to someone else. Victims pay deposits or full amounts via bank transfer only to arrive and find no accommodation. Some scammers create sophisticated fake booking websites mimicking legitimate platforms. How to avoid: Only book through official platforms like Airbnb or Booking.com. Never pay via bank transfer or cryptocurrency. Read reviews carefully. Verify property addresses on Google Maps.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — ATM Skimming and Distraction (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals install skimming devices on ATMs to capture card data and PINs. Others pose as helpful locals at ATMs or ticket machines, offering assistance while memorizing PIN codes or switching cards. An international ring was busted in 2025 after stealing over 580,000 euros across Western Europe. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours. Cover the keypad completely when entering PINs. Decline help from strangers at ATMs. Check card slots for loose attachments before inserting cards.

Scam alert in Annecy, France — Distraction Theft by Groups (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Thieves work in organized groups using distraction techniques. One person creates a diversion — asking for directions, showing a map, dropping items, staging an argument — while the others pick pockets and lift phones. They focus on tourists who are taking photos, consulting maps, or otherwise looking away from their own belongings. How to avoid: Treat any unsolicited approach by a stranger, especially a group, as a probable setup. If someone creates a scene nearby, check your belongings first, then observe. Keep your phone and wallet in front pockets or a secured pouch. Travel with a companion who can watch your back when you’re framing a shot.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — The Palais des Papes Queue Distraction (pickpocket, severity: high). Pickpocketing is the most common crime affecting tourists in Avignon. Thieves work the crowds around the Palace of the Popes, Pont d’Avignon, Place de l’Horloge, and both train stations, often in teams where one person creates a distraction while the others lift wallets and phones. Incidents climb sharply during the Festival d’Avignon in July, when the population roughly doubles overnight. How to avoid: Use a cross-body bag worn to the front with secure zippers, or a money belt worn discreetly under clothing. Never leave phones, wallets, or bags unattended. Be especially vigilant in crowds.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Petition Clipboard Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Groups of scammers, often pretending to be deaf or representing charities, approach visitors asking ‘Do you speak English?’ followed by a request to sign a petition. The petition is typically in English (suspicious in France). While you hold the clipboard, an accomplice rifles through your pockets or bags. They may also demand a donation after signing. How to avoid: Firmly say ‘non merci’ and walk away without engaging. Never hold a clipboard offered by strangers. Keep your hands free and bags secured when approached.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Fake Police Officer Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Fake officers approach tourists, flash bogus badges, and ask to inspect your passport and wallet to ‘check for counterfeit bills.’ While examining your wallet, they palm cash. Some operate under the invented title ‘Tourist Police’ to sound more official. Real French police never inspect tourists’ wallets on the street. How to avoid: Real officers only ask to see ID, never the wallet itself. Ask to see their *carte de police* clearly, and offer to walk to the nearest *commissariat* together — genuine officers will agree; scammers won’t. Do not hand over your passport or wallet. Walk toward a busy public area and dial 17 if you feel unsafe.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Taxi Overcharging (transport, severity: moderate). Unofficial taxi drivers work the Avignon TGV station and airport, offering rides at inflated rates. Even licensed taxis sometimes display the night tariff during daytime hours, claim the meter is broken, or take longer routes through town to pad the fare. How to avoid: Only use official taxis from designated taxi stands. Check that the meter shows the correct daytime tariff. Look for the official taxi sign on the roof. Use ride-hailing apps when possible.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Festival d’Avignon Crowd Scams (pickpocket, severity: high). Each July, the Festival d’Avignon swells the city by hundreds of thousands of visitors. The crowds watching street performances, queuing for shows, or pushing through packed streets create near-ideal conditions for pickpockets. Prices at street vendors also spike significantly during the festival weeks. How to avoid: Be extra vigilant during the festival period (early to late July). Keep valuables in front cross-body bags or hidden money belts. Avoid carrying large amounts of cash. Be especially careful when watching street performances.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Restaurant Tourist Trap Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Some restaurants employ deceptive pricing: giving tourists English menus with higher prices, not mentioning cheaper set menus, pushing expensive bottled water when tap water is free, adding unauthorized charges to bills, and switching to cheaper wines when premium glasses are ordered. How to avoid: Always ask for the French menu or both versions to compare. Request ‘une carafe d’eau’ for free tap water. Check if service is included. Review your bill carefully before paying.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Les Halles Market Upselling (tourist-trap, severity: low). Avignon’s covered market Les Halles has developed a reputation for inflated prices compared to other Provence markets. Vendors may employ aggressive upselling, recommending expensive items and adding products you did not request. Prices can be 3-4 times higher than comparable markets for identical products. How to avoid: Know approximate prices before shopping. Politely decline recommendations for additional items. Ask for prices before items are packaged. Visit other Provence markets for comparison.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — ATM Skimming and Card Fraud (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals install card skimming devices on ATM machines to capture card details and PIN numbers. These devices blend seamlessly with normal ATM hardware. Scammers may also use fake card slot overlays that cause your card to get stuck, then offer ‘help’ while capturing your PIN. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside banks rather than standalone machines. Cover the keypad completely when entering your PIN. Before inserting your card, inspect the machine for anything that looks crooked, loose, or damaged. Never accept help from strangers.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Friendship Bracelet Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: moderate). Scammers approach tourists and quickly weave a string bracelet around your wrist while maintaining friendly chatter. Once secured, they aggressively demand payment (often 10-20 euros). If you refuse, they may create a scene or an accomplice may use the distraction to pickpocket you. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets or crossed when approached. Firmly say ‘non’ and walk away without engaging. Never extend your hand or arm to anyone offering ‘free’ gifts. If tied, walk away without paying.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Gold Ring Scam (street-scam, severity: low). A scammer ‘finds’ a gold ring on the ground near you and offers it as your lost property or as a lucky gift. They then ask for a finder’s fee (5-20 euros). Accomplices may corroborate that the ring looks valuable. The ring is actually worthless brass. How to avoid: Simply walk away without engaging. Do not accept anything being ‘found’ near you. Ignore claims about the ring’s value or religious obligations.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Train Station Luggage Theft (theft, severity: high). Thieves board TGV and regional trains posing as passengers, wait for a distraction, and grab bags from the overhead racks before stepping off just as the doors close. At stations, they offer unsolicited help with luggage and disappear with the bag instead of carrying it. With up to 400 such incidents reported monthly on French rail, it is organized work, not opportunism. How to avoid: Keep luggage in sight at all times — ideally at your feet, not in overhead racks. Keep small valuables in a bag on your lap. Use luggage locks or a cable to tether larger bags to the rack. Decline all offers of help from strangers. Be especially alert during station stops, when most thefts occur.

Scam alert in Avignon, France — Vacation Rental Fraud (online-fraud, severity: high). Fake vacation rental scams have increased across Provence. Scammers create attractive listings offering apartments at attractive prices, then request deposits via wire transfer outside the official platform. Tourists arrive to find the property doesn’t exist or belongs to someone else. How to avoid: Book only through official platforms like Airbnb or Vrbo. Never pay outside the platform or via wire transfer. Verify host profiles and reviews carefully. Be suspicious of prices that seem too good to be true.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — Bird Droppings Pickpocket Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). You’re walking along the promenade near Grande Plage when suddenly something white and sticky lands on your shoulder. You look up instinctively, thinking it’s bird droppings. Immediately, a ‘helpful’ local appears, tutting at the pigeons and offering to help clean you up. While you’re distracted and they’re wiping your shoulder, their accomplice is emptying your pockets or bag. The ‘droppings’ are actually white paste thrown by a confederate. How to avoid: If substance lands on you, step away from any ‘helpers’ and handle it yourself. Say ‘Non, merci, ca va’ (No thanks, I’m fine) and move to a shop or restaurant to clean up. Keep wallet in a front pocket or secure crossbody bag that can’t be accessed while you’re distracted. Be suspicious of any ‘helpful stranger’ appearing instantly after an unexpected mishap.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — Beach Blanket Theft at Grande Plage (theft, severity: moderate). You’ve found a perfect spot on the golden sands of Grande Plage and left your bag and belongings on your beach towel while going for a quick swim in the Atlantic. In those few minutes, a thief has been watching and waiting. They casually stroll past your blanket, scoop up your phone, wallet, and keys in one fluid motion, and disappear into the crowd before you’ve even noticed. Beach theft spikes during July and August. How to avoid: Never leave valuables unattended on the beach — use a waterproof pouch to take essentials into the water. Leave passport, excess cash, and electronics in your hotel safe before heading to the beach. Swim in shifts with companions so someone always watches belongings. Position yourself near lifeguard stations where surveillance is higher.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — Camera Drop Scam (street-scam, severity: moderate). You’re admiring the stunning view from Rocher de la Vierge when a friendly tourist asks if you’d take their photo with their nice-looking camera. You oblige, and as you hand the camera back, they fumble it dramatically and it crashes to the ground. They examine their ‘broken’ camera and start demanding you pay for the damage — €200-300 or more. The camera was already broken or is a cheap prop. How to avoid: It’s fine to take photos for tourists, but hand the camera back carefully and step back before releasing. If they drop it, remember the fumble was on their end. Never pay cash on the spot; suggest involving police if they claim damage. Walk away if they become aggressive.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — ATM Card Skimming and Shoulder Surfing (financial-fraud, severity: high). You’re withdrawing cash from an ATM near the casino when someone approaches offering helpful advice about fees. While they ‘help,’ they’re watching you enter your PIN and may have a card skimmer in their pocket scanning your card’s magnetic strip. Or they’ve already installed a skimmer on the ATM slot itself. Days later, your account shows unauthorized withdrawals in eastern Europe. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours where tampering is less likely. Cover the keypad completely with your hand when entering your PIN. Check the card slot by wiggling it gently — skimmers are often loosely attached. Never accept help from strangers at ATMs.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — Shell Game and Three-Card Monte (gambling-scam, severity: moderate). You spot a small crowd gathered around a man with three boxes or cards on a folding table near the casino promenade. He’s shuffling them rapidly, inviting people to guess which one hides the ball. Someone in the crowd bets €20 and wins easily. But those ‘winners’ are accomplices working with the operator. The moment you put money down, sleight of hand ensures you lose. Meanwhile, pickpockets work the crowd. How to avoid: Never gamble with street operators — the games are rigged without exception. Walk past quickly without stopping to watch; observation makes you a target. Remember that every ‘winner’ you see is a plant working with the scammer. Keep hands on your valuables if you even pause near a street game.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — Friendly Bar Overcharging Scam (tourist-trap, severity: high). You’re enjoying an evening when two attractive locals strike up a friendly conversation and suggest drinks at a place they know nearby. After a couple of drinks, the bill arrives: €150-200 or more for what seemed like a few cocktails. The drinks were massively inflated ‘tourist prices,’ and your ‘friends’ chip in only a token amount before disappearing. Large bouncers may escort you to an ATM if you protest. How to avoid: Choose your own venues — never let strangers guide you to a bar they recommend. Always check prices before ordering; no posted prices is a massive red flag. Suggest well-known, established bars if new acquaintances want drinks. If confronted with an outrageous bill, insist on calling police before paying.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — Les Halles Market Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Les Halles is a beloved Biarritz institution where locals and tourists jostle to buy fresh seafood and regional specialties. The crowded aisles, sensory overload, and tourists fumbling with euros make it a prime hunting ground for skilled pickpockets. While you’re admiring the piment d’Espelette display or counting change, a bump passes unnoticed — and your wallet goes with it. How to avoid: Wear a crossbody bag with the opening against your body, hand resting on top. Keep wallet in a front pocket, never in a backpack or rear pocket. Bring only the cash you need for market purchases; leave cards at the hotel. Be extra vigilant during peak Saturday morning hours.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — Unlicensed Taxi Overcharging (transport, severity: low). You’ve just landed at Biarritz Airport after a long journey, and as you exit arrivals, a friendly man approaches offering a taxi into town. He quotes €40 — but this isn’t an official taxi. Once in the car, the price might increase, or you’re taken on a scenic route. Official airport taxis should cost around €25 to central Biarritz. Unlicensed operators charge double or triple the standard fare. How to avoid: Use only official taxis from the designated taxi rank at the airport or station. Look for official taxi signage, license numbers on windshield, and running meters. Know the expected fare in advance: airport to city center is approximately €25. Use ride-hailing apps for transparent pricing.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — Fake Charity Petition Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). You’re strolling along the promenade when a young woman approaches with a clipboard, gesturing that she’s deaf-mute. She wants you to sign a petition for disabled children or another worthy cause. Once signed, she flips to a donation page showing €20-50 amounts. Meanwhile, your attention is on the clipboard, making you an easy mark for an accomplice to pickpocket. The charity doesn’t exist. How to avoid: Politely decline with ‘Non, merci’ and keep walking without breaking stride. Never sign anything on the street; legitimate charities don’t solicit signatures on promenades. Keep your hands occupied with bags or phone so you can’t take the clipboard. Genuine charities have websites, offices, and don’t rely on street solicitation.

Scam alert in Biarritz, France — Remote Beach and Parking Lot Car Break-Ins (theft, severity: moderate). You drive to one of Biarritz’s remote surf beaches for an afternoon in the water. You leave the rental car in the parking lot with your bags hidden in the trunk. But thieves stake out these beach parking areas, watching tourists head down to the water. Within minutes, they’ve smashed a window or popped the lock — and valuables ‘hidden’ in the trunk get found in under a minute. How to avoid: Leave everything of value at your hotel; don’t bring anything to the beach you can’t carry into the water. Use paid, supervised lots rather than remote free parking whenever the option exists. If you must leave items in the car, load the trunk before you arrive, never in the lot. Don’t leave any bag visible, even if it contains nothing worth taking.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — The Miroir d'Eau Photo Distraction (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Pickpockets operate in crowded tourist areas throughout Bordeaux, particularly at Place de la Bourse, along Rue Sainte-Catherine (one of Europe’s longest pedestrian shopping streets), and near the Miroir d’Eau. Thieves work in teams, using distraction techniques while accomplices steal wallets, phones, and valuables. They often target tourists who are taking photos or consulting maps. How to avoid: Use an anti-theft bag with hidden compartments. Keep your wallet in a front pocket, never a back one. Skip the conspicuous jewelry and electronics on Rue Sainte-Catherine. Stay alert in the crowds, and keep bags zipped and worn in front of your body.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — Train Station Theft (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Gare Saint-Jean attracts pickpockets who target tourists carrying luggage. A common tactic involves groups of four to six people pushing onto trains right before the doors close, crowding their target while accomplices lift valuables, and stepping off just as the doors shut. Others work the ticket machines and crowded platforms. How to avoid: Keep bags zipped and in front of you. Be extra vigilant when boarding — the last-second rush is the telltale setup. Don’t carry phones or wallets in easily accessible pockets. Treat anyone pressing unusually close as a warning sign. Board early rather than at the last moment; the crush is the cover.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — The Petition Clipboard Scam (distraction, severity: low). Scammers approach tourists with clipboards asking them to sign a petition, often claiming to support deaf children or a charitable cause. While the tourist is distracted reading and signing, an accomplice steals their wallet, phone, or valuables from bags or pockets. Sometimes the petitioner themselves will demand a donation after signing, becoming aggressive if refused. How to avoid: Politely decline and keep walking. Never stop for clipboard solicitors. Keep hands on your belongings. Say ‘non merci’ firmly while continuing to move. Never sign anything on the street.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — The Friendship Bracelet Trap (distraction, severity: low). A stranger approaches and begins tying a colorful string bracelet on your wrist as a supposed ‘gift’ or sign of friendship. Once the bracelet is tied, they aggressively demand payment, often 10-20 euros. They refuse to take the bracelet back and may create a scene to pressure payment. Meanwhile, accomplices may use the distraction to pickpocket you. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets or crossed. Firmly refuse any ‘gifts’ from strangers. Say ‘non’ and walk away quickly. Never let strangers touch your hands or wrists. If a bracelet is tied, refuse to pay and walk toward police.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — The Gold Ring Trick (distraction, severity: low). A scammer pretends to ‘find’ a gold ring on the ground near you and insists you should have it, claiming it doesn’t fit them or suggesting you can sell it. They then ask for a small finder’s fee or payment. The ring is worthless brass or fake gold. This scam is particularly common throughout France and targets tourists who appear kind or confused. How to avoid: Ignore anyone who approaches with a ‘found’ ring. Keep walking without engaging. Say ‘Ce n’est pas à moi’ (It’s not mine) and walk away. Remember that real gold rings are never given away by strangers.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — Fake Police Wallet Inspection (impersonation, severity: high). Scammers posing as plainclothes officers flash fake badges and demand to inspect your wallet for ‘counterfeit currency.’ They work in pairs: one plays a drug dealer or a lost tourist to engage you first, and the fake officer appears moments later to ‘investigate.’ While examining your cash, they palm bills. Real French police never inspect wallets on the street. How to avoid: Real officers only ask to see ID, never the wallet itself. Ask to see their *carte de police* and offer to walk to the nearest *commissariat* together — genuine police will comply. Dial 17 if you are unsure. Do not hand over your wallet to anyone on the street, regardless of uniform.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — Unlicensed Taxi Overcharging (transport, severity: moderate). Unlicensed taxi drivers approach tourists at Bordeaux-Mérignac Airport and Gare Saint-Jean offering rides at inflated prices. A common line is that there’s a taxi strike, or that official taxis are unavailable — both usually untrue. These drivers charge two to three times the normal fare and often carry no commercial insurance. Some work with rigged meters, or simply claim the meter is broken. How to avoid: Only use taxis from official taxi ranks. Look for vehicles with official taxi signage and roof lights. Use ride-sharing apps like Uber or Bolt for transparent pricing. Always confirm the fare before getting in. Note the driver’s license number displayed in the vehicle.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — Restaurant Menu Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Some restaurants in tourist areas show tourists different menus with higher prices, add hidden charges for bread, water, or table settings, or charge for items not ordered. Staff may also substitute cheaper wine when premium glasses are ordered. Bills may include undisclosed service charges or inflated prices for tourists, especially Americans. How to avoid: Check that menus display prices (legally required in France). Compare printed menu prices to your bill. Ask ‘une carafe d’eau’ for free tap water. Verify wine bottle labels match what you ordered. Avoid restaurants without posted prices.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — ATM Skimming and Card Theft (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals install skimming devices on ATMs to capture card details and PINs. These devices blend with the ATM’s original hardware and are hard to detect. Scammers also use distraction techniques: one person engages you while another watches you enter your PIN or manipulates the machine to trap your card. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours. Inspect card slots for loose attachments. Cover keypad when entering PIN. Never accept help from strangers at ATMs. If card is trapped, don’t leave and call your bank immediately.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — Rose Seller Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: low). Men approach couples or women at restaurant terraces and outdoor cafes, offering a ‘free’ rose as a romantic gesture. Once the rose is accepted or touched, they aggressively demand payment of 5-10 euros. They refuse to take the rose back and create uncomfortable confrontations. Sometimes accomplices use this distraction to pickpocket victims. How to avoid: Decline firmly and keep your hands away. Avoid touching offered items. Say ‘non merci’ without stopping. Alert restaurant staff if sellers become aggressive.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — Tram and Bus Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Pickpockets operate on Bordeaux’s tram network and buses, particularly during rush hours and on routes serving tourist areas. Thieves create distractions by bumping into victims or ‘helping’ with bags while accomplices steal valuables. At stops near tourist destinations, thieves may grab phones or bags just as doors are closing. How to avoid: Keep valuables in front pockets or secure inside bags. Stay alert especially near doors. Be wary of anyone offering unsolicited help. Avoid standing near doors with easily accessible items.

Scam alert in Bordeaux, France — Fake Accommodation Listings (online-fraud, severity: high). Scammers create fake Airbnb or rental listings using photos from legitimate properties, offering attractive prices in desirable locations. They request payment via wire transfer or cryptocurrency outside the official platform, then disappear. Tourists arrive to find the property doesn’t exist or belongs to someone else. France is a hotspot for this scam. How to avoid: Only book through official platforms and pay through their systems. Be suspicious of unusually low prices. Never wire money directly. Verify listings have reviews and host history. Use Google Street View to verify property exists.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Luxury Watch Theft (robbery, severity: high). Organized crews target tourists wearing watches worth over €100,000. Spotters on La Croisette and around luxury hotel terraces identify Rolexes, Patek Philippes, and Audemars Piguets, then signal to accomplices who rip the watch off the wrist and flee on mopeds with tampered plates. In 2024 the Alpes-Maritimes region recorded 301 stolen watches totaling €8.3 million. Attacks can involve tear gas and have turned violent when victims resist. How to avoid: Leave expensive watches at home or in your hotel safe. If you must wear one, keep it concealed under long sleeves. Be especially vigilant on restaurant terraces and near luxury hotels. Sit with your back to the wall when dining.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Taxi Meter Manipulation (transport, severity: moderate). Despite fixed rates from Nice Airport (€85 to Cannes), some taxi drivers start with the fixed rate already on the meter and then let it continue running, effectively charging double. Drivers may claim credit card machines are broken to force cash payment without a receipt, enabling overcharging. How to avoid: Confirm the fixed rate before entering the taxi and photograph the meter at the start. Insist on a receipt and credit card payment. Use official taxi ranks at the airport. Consider Uber where available.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Pickpocketing with Distraction (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Professional pickpockets work Cannes in teams of three or more: one person creates a distraction — asking directions, spilling a drink, staging an argument — while the others lift wallets and phones. Crowds around the Palais des Festivals and boarding platforms at Cannes train station are where most incidents happen. How to avoid: Carry a money belt or anti-theft crossbody bag and keep wallets in front pockets. Treat any unsolicited approach as a possible setup, especially in tight crowds. If a drink or sauce lands on you, step away from any ‘helper’ before addressing it — that’s when pockets go empty.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Petition and Charity Clipboard Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Scammers, often pretending to be deaf and mute, approach tourists with clipboards asking them to sign petitions for fake charities. After signing, they demand donations of €2-10. While your hands are occupied signing, accomplices may pickpocket your belongings. How to avoid: Politely but firmly decline and keep walking. Never sign anything presented by strangers on the street. Keep your hands free and your belongings secured.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Gold Ring Scam (street-scam, severity: low). A stranger bends down near you, picks up what looks like a gold ring, and offers to sell it to you at a discount — it’s marked ‘18K’ and they ‘need money right now.’ The ring is brass or copper stamped to look valuable, worth pennies. The urgency is the tell. How to avoid: Do not buy jewelry from strangers on the street, ever. If someone presses a ‘found’ ring toward you, say *non* and keep walking. Touching the ring is what starts the script — keep your hands occupied or in pockets.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Friendship Bracelet Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: low). Scammers approach tourists and quickly tie colorful string bracelets around their wrists, making them difficult to remove. They then aggressively demand payment of €10-20. While the victim is distracted, an accomplice may steal wallets or phones. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets or crossed when approached by street vendors. Firmly say ‘Non, merci’ and walk away immediately.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Beach Club Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Some private beach clubs add unauthorized charges to bills, including inflated prices for basic items. Staff may aggressively enforce rules about outside food, confiscating items and pressuring customers to buy expensive alternatives. Hidden ‘service charges’ may appear on final bills. How to avoid: Ask for a complete price list before ordering and confirm all charges upfront. Keep all receipts and check your bill carefully before paying. Choose established beach clubs with good reviews.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Restaurant Menu Tricks (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Some restaurants use deceptive pricing including dual menus with higher prices for tourists, omitting prices for daily specials that turn out expensive, and adding unauthorized cover charges. Fish may be priced per 100 grams rather than per portion, leading to shocking bills. How to avoid: Ask for the price of every verbal special before ordering. Request a menu that shows prices in writing. *Service compris* means service is included — any extra ‘service charge’ line is not owed. Read recent reviews before committing.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Fake Police Officer Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Criminals pose as plainclothes police officers and approach tourists, claiming to conduct ID or currency checks. They ask to see your wallet to ‘verify’ your money isn’t counterfeit, then steal cash or the entire wallet. Real French police rarely approach tourists on the street for such checks. How to avoid: Legitimate French police almost never approach tourists for random currency checks. Never hand over your wallet. Ask to see police credentials and suggest going to a police station together. Call 17 if threatened.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — ATM Skimming and Shimming (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals install nearly invisible ‘shimming’ devices inside ATM card slots that capture data from your card’s chip. These devices use Bluetooth or cellular connections to transmit stolen data. Some criminals also install hidden cameras to capture PIN codes. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside banks during banking hours. Cover the keypad when entering your PIN. Inspect the card slot for anything loose or unusual. Enable transaction alerts on your accounts.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Vacation Rental Fraud (online-fraud, severity: high). Scammers create fake listings for properties that don’t exist or aren’t available, using stolen photos. They insist on payment outside official platforms like Airbnb. Victims discover upon arrival that their reservation doesn’t exist. Particularly common during the Film Festival when demand peaks. How to avoid: Only book through reputable platforms and never pay outside the official system. Be suspicious of prices significantly below market rate, especially during Film Festival. Verify listings have reviews.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Film Festival Credential Scams (online-fraud, severity: moderate). Fake websites and social media accounts offer Film Festival passes, party invitations, or screening tickets at inflated prices for events that don’t exist. Scammers also target filmmakers with fake festivals charging high submission fees. Some fake internship programs charge thousands for worthless ‘festival experience’ programs. How to avoid: Purchase tickets and passes only through official Cannes Film Festival channels (festival-cannes.com). Research any festival carefully before paying fees. Verify internship programs through educational institutions.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Yacht Charter Fraud (online-fraud, severity: high). Fraudulent yacht charter companies advertise luxury boats they don’t own, taking large deposits and disappearing. Warning signs include companies with only mobile phone contacts, no physical address, pressure to pay quickly, and unusually low prices. How to avoid: Book only with established charter companies with physical offices. Verify membership in professional organizations like MYBA or ECPY. Never pay large deposits to unverified companies. Meet the boat and crew before final payment if possible.

Scam alert in Cannes, France — Car Break-In Theft (theft, severity: high). Thieves target rental cars parked at beaches, hiking trailheads, and tourist sites, recognizing rental vehicles by their license plates. They break windows to steal valuables in seconds, targeting cameras, electronics, luggage, and passports. How to avoid: Never leave anything visible in your car. Remove all belongings when parking, even briefly. Use monitored parking garages rather than street parking. Keep important documents on your person.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Fake Chalet Rental Scam (online-fraud, severity: high). Scammers screenshot photos of legitimate luxury chalets and create fake listings at suspiciously low prices during peak winter season. They request immediate wire transfers for deposits and first month’s rent, often claiming high demand requires fast action. Once payment is sent, the scammer disappears and victims arrive to find the property either doesn’t exist or is occupied by the real owner. This is the most widespread scam affecting visitors to Chamonix. How to avoid: Book through established agencies like Chamonix All Year or verified platforms. Never wire money to individuals without seeing the property. Use credit cards for payment protection. Verify property addresses on Google Street View. Join local Facebook groups like Cham Social for recommendations.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Unlicensed Mountain Guide Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Fake ‘mountain guides’ advertise online with fabricated testimonials and impressive-sounding credentials, charging €1,500 or more for Mont Blanc summit attempts. These unqualified operators have abandoned exhausted clients in dangerous conditions near high-altitude refuges, leaving them stranded in snowstorms. Without proper insurance, clients have no recourse for compensation when accidents happen — and in the Alps, accidents happen. How to avoid: Book only through Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix or IFMGA-certified guides. Ask to see the guide’s UIAGM/IFMGA identification card. Verify guide credentials on official mountain guide registries. Use established mountain guiding companies with insurance guarantees.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Fake Ski Instructor Scam (impersonation, severity: moderate). Unqualified individuals pose as ski instructors online, offering lessons at discounted rates compared to ESF (École du Ski Français). Some take advance payment and never appear, while others actually conduct lessons without proper certification. Victims who take lessons from unqualified instructors face serious safety risks on challenging Alpine terrain and have no insurance coverage. French courts have fined operators over €26,000 for employing unlicensed instructors. How to avoid: Book through ESF Chamonix or other licensed ski schools. Verify instructor certifications through official channels. Ask for proof of insurance before lessons begin. Check reviews on established booking platforms.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Ski Equipment Theft at Slopes (theft, severity: moderate). Opportunistic thieves work the ski racks outside mountain restaurants and lodges, targeting expensive gear left unattended. The ‘snatch and grab’ accounts for roughly 90% of ski thefts: the thief walks past once to spot desirable equipment, then returns moments later to take it. High-end skis, boots, and poles worth thousands of euros disappear inside the ten minutes you’re waiting for your *tartiflette*. How to avoid: Use ski locks with cables at least 4mm thick. Separate your skis and store them in different rack locations. Leave skis in less crowded areas away from main entrances. Use resort locker facilities like Skicase in Chamonix. Purchase rental insurance that covers theft.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Booking Platform Accommodation Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Guests book legitimate-appearing properties through major platforms but encounter unexpected demands upon arrival. In documented Chamonix cases, hosts have held guests ‘hostage’ demanding additional cash deposits of €400 or more that were never mentioned in the listing and never returned. Some properties advertised as ski-in/ski-out turn out to be far from slopes. How to avoid: Only communicate and pay through official booking platform channels. Read all reviews carefully, especially recent negative ones. Verify exact property location on maps before booking. Document all communications and demands in writing. Report unusual demands immediately to the booking platform.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Defective SIM Card Scam (street-scam, severity: low). Tourists purchase prepaid SIM cards marketed as 5G service with 14 days of calls and data for €34. The SIM cards stop working within hours of purchase, and when customers contact the carrier (such as Orange), they discover the SIM was already deactivated or never properly activated. Shop owners claim no responsibility. How to avoid: Purchase SIM cards from official carrier stores (Orange, SFR, Bouygues). Ask seller to activate and test the SIM before completing purchase. Keep all receipts and packaging. Consider purchasing SIM cards at Geneva Airport before arrival.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Unlicensed Airport Transfer Overcharging (transport, severity: moderate). Unofficial taxi drivers approach tourists at Geneva Airport offering transfers to Chamonix at seemingly reasonable rates. Once en route, they demand significantly higher fees, sometimes claiming the original quote was per person not per vehicle, or adding fuel surcharges and border crossing fees. Some drivers refuse to cross into France, abandoning passengers at the border. How to avoid: Pre-book transfers through established companies like Alpine Fleet or Chamonix Cabs. Use official shared shuttle services (€30-40 per person). Get written confirmation of total price including all fees. Book private transfers that average €150-200 for the journey.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Gold Ring Scam (street-scam, severity: low). A person ‘finds’ a gold ring on the ground near you and offers to sell it at a ‘discounted’ price since they don’t need it. The ring is actually worthless brass or plated metal. While this scam is more common in Paris and larger French cities, it appears in mountain resort towns during peak season when wealthy tourists are concentrated. How to avoid: Politely refuse and walk away immediately. Never engage in conversation about found items. Understand that real gold rings aren’t sold by strangers on streets.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Fake Police Officer Scam (impersonation, severity: moderate). Individuals impersonate plainclothes police and approach tourists claiming to conduct anti-counterfeiting operations or security checks. They ask to see ID, wallets, or bag contents, and use the opportunity to palm cash, cards, or valuables. Some work in teams — one distracts with the ‘check’ while another pickpockets. How to avoid: Ask to see official police credentials. Offer to accompany them to the nearest police station. Never hand over your wallet — show ID through clear wallet pocket. Call 17 (French police) if suspicious.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Counterfeit Ski Pass Sales (street-scam, severity: moderate). Scammers sell counterfeit or stolen ski passes at discounted prices, either online before arrival or near lift stations. These passes may be altered legitimate passes with dates whited out, child passes being sold for adult use, or completely counterfeited tickets. Victims are caught at lift gates, face fines up to €999, and lose their payment. How to avoid: Purchase passes only from official Compagnie du Mont-Blanc outlets. Buy online through official Chamonix lift company website. Never buy passes from individuals at the resort. Keep receipts as proof of legitimate purchase.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Cable Car Crowding Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: low). During peak season, the famous cable cars become extremely crowded with tourists focused on the views outside. Pickpockets take advantage of the tight quarters and distracted passengers to lift wallets, phones, and valuables. The Aiguille du Midi cable car, which packs up to 65 passengers into a small cabin, is particularly vulnerable on the way up to 3,842 meters. How to avoid: Keep valuables in front pockets or secure money belt. Use bags with zippers worn across your body in front. Be extra vigilant during boarding and crowded moments. Leave unnecessary valuables in hotel safe.

Scam alert in Chamonix, France — Restaurant Tourist Trap Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: low). Some restaurants in prime tourist locations employ tactics to overcharge visitors: presenting menus without prices, automatically adding expensive bottled water instead of free tap water, charging inflated ‘terrace supplements,’ adding undisclosed service charges, or bringing unrequested items and then charging premium prices. How to avoid: Always request a menu with prices before ordering. Ask specifically for ‘une carafe d’eau’ (tap water) which is free. Confirm prices for daily specials before ordering. Check the bill carefully before paying.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — Train Station Luggage Helper Theft (theft, severity: high). Organized groups of thieves operate at Colmar train station, posing as helpful strangers offering to assist tourists with their luggage. Two or three young individuals approach travelers on stairs or near platforms, insisting on helping carry bags despite refusals. While one person distracts with conversation or blocks your view, another rifles through bags or pockets, stealing passports, wallets, and valuables. How to avoid: Firmly decline all unsolicited help with luggage. Ask station staff in red tabards for assistance if needed. Keep bags zipped and secured in front of your body. Travel with only luggage you can manage alone.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — Christmas Market Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: moderate). During Colmar’s famous Christmas markets (late November through December), professional pickpockets work the dense crowds moving between market stalls. Victims often report having wallets stolen from zipped crossbody purses or coat pockets while navigating the narrow medieval streets packed with holiday shoppers. The crush of tourists photographing half-timbered houses creates perfect cover for skilled thieves. How to avoid: Wear crossbody bags in front of your body with locking zippers. Keep wallets in front pockets or money belts under clothing. Visit markets Monday-Thursday when crowds are lighter. Avoid peak weekend hours between 11am-5pm.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — Restaurant Tourist Menu Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Certain restaurants in Colmar’s heavily-touristed areas engage in deceptive pricing practices. Visitors have reported being charged 7 euros extra per person when attempting to share a menu. Other tactics include presenting tourists with different menus featuring inflated prices, adding undisclosed charges for bread or water, or bringing unrequested items and billing for them. How to avoid: Check prices on posted menus before sitting down. Eat where locals eat — venture a few streets from main tourist paths. Review recent TripAdvisor and Google reviews before dining. Ask for itemized bill and verify all charges match menu prices.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — Fake Petition/Deaf Charity Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Groups of individuals approach tourists with clipboards, asking them to sign petitions for fake charitable causes, often pretending to be deaf-mute. The petitions are typically in English (suspicious in a French city) and claim to support disabled people. After signing, they reveal a ‘donation’ column and pressure you for 10-20 euros. While you’re distracted, an accomplice may be pickpocketing you. How to avoid: Say ‘Non, merci’ firmly and keep walking without stopping. Never sign anything offered by strangers on the street. Keep your bag secured in front of you if approached. Remember that legitimate charities don’t solicit cash on streets.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — ATM Skimming and Card Fraud (financial-fraud, severity: high). France experiences 42% of all European bank card fraud. Criminals install skimming devices on ATMs that capture card data and hidden cameras or keypad overlays that record PIN entries. Tourist areas are prime targets because foreign cards are less likely to have advanced security features. Victims typically discover the theft weeks later when unauthorized charges appear on their statements. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours only. Inspect the card slot and keypad before inserting card — wiggle the slot. Always cover your hand when entering PIN. Set up transaction alerts on your cards before traveling.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — Fake Police Officer Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Scammers pose as plainclothes police officers, quickly flashing fake badges and demanding to ‘check your documents and wallet for counterfeit currency.’ While examining your wallet, they palm cash or memorize card details. Some wear partial uniforms or hats with police markings to appear legitimate. French authorities have warned about increased incidents of criminals impersonating officers. How to avoid: Real French police will never demand your wallet, cash, or phone. Ask to see their *carte de police* and note the badge number. Offer to walk to the nearest *commissariat* together for any document check — genuine officers will comply; scammers won’t. Dial 17 if you’re unsure.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — QR Code Parking Meter Scam (Quishing) (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). Scammers place fake QR code stickers over legitimate ones on parking meters throughout France. When tourists scan the fraudulent code, they’re directed to a convincing phishing website that mimics official parking payment services. Victims enter their license plate, parking duration, and credit card details — all captured by criminals. Some victims are tricked into entering multiple card numbers after being told their payment ‘failed.’ How to avoid: Run your finger over QR codes to detect if it’s a sticker covering another code. Type parking payment URLs directly rather than scanning codes. Use official parking apps downloaded from app stores, not QR links. Pay at meter using coin or chip-enabled card rather than QR when possible.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — Wine Tasting Pressure Sales (tourist-trap, severity: low). While wine tastings along the Alsace Wine Route often appear free, there’s strong social pressure to purchase bottles afterward. Some establishments serve generous pours to lower inhibitions, create false scarcity (‘last bottles of this vintage’), or make tourists feel obligated after extensive tastings. Staff may become noticeably cold or hostile if visitors don’t make purchases. How to avoid: Look for ‘Vignobles et Decouvertes’ certified wineries for quality assurance. Set a budget before entering any cave and stick to it. Know it’s perfectly acceptable to taste and buy just one bottle or none at all. Ask about tasting fees upfront before sampling begins.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — Rental Car Break-In Theft (theft, severity: moderate). Thieves specifically target rental cars parked at tourist attractions throughout Alsace. They watch parking lots for tourists who open their trunks to store or retrieve items, marking which vehicles contain valuables. Rental cars are easily identified by registration stickers, missing floor mats, and clean interiors. Travelers return from wine tastings to find windows smashed and all belongings stolen. How to avoid: Don’t open your trunk in the parking lot where thieves can see the contents. Retrieve what you need a kilometer before you arrive. Clear out visible items — guidebooks, maps, ticket stubs, rental paperwork — before you park. Use underground or multi-story garages with CCTV when the option exists.

Scam alert in Colmar, France — Fake Accommodation Booking Scam (online-fraud, severity: high). Scammers create fake listings that mimic real Colmar properties on platforms like Airbnb and Booking.com, or send phishing emails claiming your reservation was canceled and demanding large penalty charges. Colmar’s picture-perfect half-timbered houses make it easy to steal convincing photos. Victims arrive to find their ‘charming Alsatian apartment’ doesn’t exist. How to avoid: Book only through official platforms and pay within their secure system. Verify emails by logging into booking sites directly, never via email links. Cross-reference property photos using reverse image search. Read reviews carefully and look for specific details about Colmar location.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — The Part-Dieu Metro Bag-Swarm (pickpocket, severity: high). Pickpockets in Lyon work the tourist-heavy areas and crowded public transport, usually in teams: one person asks for directions, bumps into you, or stages a scene while the others lift your wallet or phone. At the Confluence tram stop, groups of women carrying oversized bags have been observed surrounding tourists to get at backpacks. On Métro Line D and the T2 tram, thefts cluster around rush-hour boarding and exiting when movement is chaotic enough to mask the lift. How to avoid: Wear bags across your body with zippers facing inward. Keep only minimal cash and one card on you. Use money belts or hidden pouches. Stay alert during metro boarding and exiting.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Fake Metro Ticket Scam (fraud, severity: moderate). Ticket touts approach tourists who appear lost or confused at major Lyon train stations. They offer to sell metro tickets at seemingly reasonable prices, but the tickets are either fake, expired, or already used. The scammer may claim they have ‘extra’ tickets or offer a ‘discount’ compared to the official ticket machines. When you try to use the ticket, it won’t work at the turnstile. How to avoid: Only buy tickets from official TCL machines or counters. Use the TCL mobile app for digital tickets. Ignore anyone offering to sell tickets outside official channels.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Fake Charity/Petition Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Someone approaches along Rue de la République with a clipboard and opens with ‘Do you speak English?’ They want you to sign a petition for a deaf-mute charity. Once you’ve signed, they flip to a donation column and pressure you for cash — while your attention is on the clipboard, an accomplice is often working your bag from behind. The charity is fake. How to avoid: Simply say ‘Non, merci’ and keep walking. Never sign anything handed to you on the street. Legitimate charities in France only ask for email addresses, not cash.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Restaurant Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Tourist-centric restaurants near Lyon’s historic areas may present inflated bills. Tactics include: adding items you didn’t order, charging for bread and water that appeared ‘free,’ using ‘tourist menus’ with elevated prices. Some establishments trade on Lyon’s reputation as France’s gastronomic capital to justify excessive prices for mediocre food. How to avoid: Check prices before sitting down. Ask for itemized bills and review carefully. Eat where locals eat, away from main tourist streets.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Shell Game / Three-Card Monte (gambling-scam, severity: high). A scammer sets up a makeshift table with three cups or cards. They invite you to bet on guessing the ball’s location. ‘Winners’ in the crowd are accomplices who pretend to win to draw you in. The game is completely rigged through sleight of hand — you cannot win. How to avoid: Never play street gambling games — they are always rigged. Do not stop to watch. Remember that bystanders are likely accomplices.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Gold Ring Scam (street-scam, severity: low). A person ‘finds’ a gold ring on the ground near you and asks if you dropped it. When you say no, they show you a marking claiming it’s real gold and offer to sell it for a ‘good price.’ The ring is worthless brass. They may also ask for money ‘for food’ or ‘for their children.’ How to avoid: Don’t engage — say ‘Non’ and keep walking. Never accept items ‘found’ on the street.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Friendship Bracelet Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: moderate). A vendor grabs your hand in Vieux Lyon and weaves a colorful string bracelet around your wrist, finishing with a knot you can’t untie. Then they demand €10–€20. If you refuse, they become aggressive — and in the confrontation, an accomplice often works your pockets. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets when approached. Say ‘Non’ firmly and keep walking. Don’t let anyone touch you or attach anything.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Rose/Flower Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: low). A seller approaches couples dining outdoors, offering a rose with ‘Flower for the pretty lady!’ The moment you touch or accept the flower, they demand 5-10 euros. If you try to return it, they refuse and become aggressive until you pay out of embarrassment. How to avoid: Don’t touch or accept any flowers offered. A simple ‘Non, merci’ and wave sends them away. Ask restaurant staff to intervene if needed.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Fake Police Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Criminals pose as plainclothes police, flash fake badges, and say they need to check your wallet for counterfeit bills or ‘drug money.’ While examining the cash, they palm bills. Sometimes a ‘lost tourist’ accomplice has just asked you to break a large note, and the fake officer arrives moments later claiming street currency exchange is illegal. How to avoid: Real officers only ask to see ID, never the wallet. Ask to see their *carte de police* and offer to walk to the nearest *commissariat* together — genuine police will comply; scammers won’t. Dial 17 if something feels off.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Taxi Overcharging (transport, severity: moderate). Some taxi drivers take advantage of tourists unfamiliar with Lyon’s layout. They take long routes to inflate the fare, ‘forget’ to start the meter, or select the higher night or weekend tariff during regular hours. Airport runs are particularly vulnerable — the legitimate fare from Lyon-Saint Exupéry to the city center is around €50–€70. How to avoid: Only use taxis from official ranks. Ensure the meter is zeroed before departure. Use GPS on your phone to follow the route. Consider using Uber or Bolt.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — ATM Skimming / Private ATM Scam (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals attach skimming devices to ATMs that steal your card data and PIN. Private ATM companies like Euronet place machines that charge excessive fees and poor exchange rates — up to 4x more than bank ATMs. They may offer Dynamic Currency Conversion at terrible rates. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside bank branches only. Look for major French banks: BNP Paribas, Société Générale, LCL. Always cover keypad when entering PIN. Decline dynamic currency conversion.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Broken Camera Scam (fraud, severity: low). Someone asks you to take their photo using their camera. After you return the camera, they claim you broke it and demand money for repairs. The ‘camera’ was already broken — they use it repeatedly for this scam. How to avoid: Politely decline to take photos with others’ cameras. If accused of damage, suggest filing a police report together — scammers will refuse.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Friendship Bracelet/String Scam (distraction, severity: low). Someone approaches you in a friendly manner on Vieux-Port and loops a colored string or bracelet around your wrist before you can refuse. Once it’s tied, they call it a ‘gift’ and aggressively demand cash — typically €5–€20. They may physically grab your wrist to tie it, and if you try to walk off without paying, they make a scene to pressure you into handing over the money. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets when walking through Vieux-Port and La Canebière. Say *non merci* firmly and keep moving. Do not stop to engage. If they grab your wrist, pull your hand away and walk toward a busy shop or café — they rarely follow.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Gold Ring Scam (distraction, severity: low). A passer-by ‘finds’ a gold ring on the ground near you and picks it up, showing it to you and claiming it’s yours or that you must have dropped it. When you say it’s not yours, they offer to let you have it as it ‘must be your lucky day.’ They then ask for a reward or ‘finder’s fee’ for their ‘honesty.’ The ring is actually cheap brass or gold-plated and worthless, worth perhaps a few cents. How to avoid: Ignore anyone who approaches claiming to have found something valuable. Say ‘Non, ce n’est pas à moi’ (No, it’s not mine) and walk away. Never accept items from strangers. Do not engage in conversation about found items.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Marseille has significant pickpocket activity, especially in tourist areas. Thieves work in groups using distraction techniques. Common methods: children swarming tourists near Gare Saint-Charles while accomplices lift valuables; one person asking for directions while another picks the pocket; staged bumps and commotions; and tight crowding at Metro doors timed so the thief grabs and steps off as the doors close. The concentration around Gare Saint-Charles is particularly heavy. How to avoid: Wear a cross-body bag in front, not behind. Keep phones out of back pockets. Never sling a bag over a chair back at outdoor tables. Use a money belt for large amounts of cash and cards. Be extra vigilant when metro doors open and close. Avoid displaying expensive watches, cameras, or jewelry. Keep only what you need for the day; leave valuables in hotel safe.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Fake Charity Petition Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). A person approaches with a clipboard, often claiming to be deaf-mute, and asks if you speak English. They then request you sign a ‘petition’ for a charity, supposedly supporting deaf or disabled people. The petition is in English (a red flag in France) and looks official. After signing, they demand a donation, pointing to text on the paper claiming you agreed to donate when you signed. While you’re distracted signing, an accomplice may be going through your pockets or bag. Even if there’s no accomplice, you may feel pressured into giving money for a fake cause. How to avoid: Never stop for clipboard petitioners. Say ‘Non’ firmly and keep walking. Never sign anything on the street. Keep hands in pockets and maintain distance. If approached, check that your belongings are secure immediately.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Three Card Monte / Shell Game (street-scam, severity: moderate). You encounter a group gathered around someone playing a simple card game (find the queen) or shell game (find the ball under the cup). The game looks easy to win, and you watch people (who are actually accomplices called ‘shills’) winning money easily. When you try to play, you lose every time because the operator uses sleight of hand to cheat. The game depends on a lookout watching for police, a ‘roper’ to bring in players, and shills who pretend to win. The moment you put down money, it’s gone. Some operations may become aggressive if you try to leave without paying. How to avoid: Never play street gambling games — they are always rigged. Do not stop to watch. Remember that bystanders are likely accomplices. The shell game is fraud in France.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Taxi Overcharging / Unlicensed Taxi Scam (transport, severity: moderate). Unlicensed taxi drivers or unscrupulous licensed drivers target tourists arriving at the airport or train station. They may refuse to use the meter, quote a fixed price that’s significantly inflated, take unnecessarily long routes, or claim the meter is broken. Some unlicensed operators solicit fares inside terminals. At night, prices can be quoted at 2-3x the normal rate. Official airport-to-city fare should be approximately 50 euros daytime and 60 euros at night. How to avoid: Use only official taxis from designated ranks (outside Arrivals Hall at airport). Confirm the fare before getting in. Insist on the meter being used. Know the approximate fare in advance (€50 day/€60 night airport to center). Use ride-sharing apps like Uber for transparent pricing. Note driver ID and license plate if overcharged — report to police.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Restaurant Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Restaurants in tourist areas use a familiar playbook: posted prices that don’t match the bill; verbal ‘specials’ that turn out to be expensive; items added that you didn’t order; bottled water served automatically when you ask for water; pressure for American-style tips despite service being included; only medium or large sizes offered at inflated prices; and a different, higher-priced menu for tourists than for locals. One documented Marseille case showed a €28 menu where 9 of 13 dishes required a €5–€10 supplement each. How to avoid: Ask for the French menu and compare prices. Request ‘une carafe d’eau’ (pitcher of tap water) — it’s free. Verify prices for specials before ordering. Review the bill carefully (‘l’addition’) against what you ordered. Tipping is not required in France — service is included. Choose restaurants away from main tourist thoroughfares. Read recent online reviews.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — ATM Skimming / Card Trap Scam (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals fit skimming hardware onto ATMs to capture your card data and PIN: an overlay over the card slot reads the magnetic stripe, a fake keypad or pinhole camera records your PIN, and in the card-trap variant a false insert jams the card inside. In that version, a ‘helpful’ stranger appears and watches you re-enter the PIN a few times; once you leave to find help, they retrieve the card and use it with the code they just learned. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside bank branches during business hours. Cover the keypad completely when entering your PIN. Wiggle the card slot and the keypad before inserting your card — skimmers are usually loosely attached. If your card gets stuck, do not leave the machine; call the bank number printed on it. Decline help from any stranger at an ATM, and enable transaction alerts before you leave home.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Fake Police Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Two people in official-looking uniforms or plain clothes approach you, flash fake badges quickly, and claim to be ‘Tourist Police’ or plainclothes officers. They claim they need to check your wallet for counterfeit bills, ‘drug money,’ or verify your identity. While examining your wallet, they discreetly remove bills. They may also ask to see your passport and credit cards. By the time you realize money is missing, they’ve disappeared. Some variations involve accusing you of a minor infraction and demanding an immediate ‘fine’ paid in cash. How to avoid: Real French police never check tourists’ wallets on the street. Ask to see ID clearly and note badge number. Insist on going to the nearest police station before handing anything over. Never give your wallet to anyone on the street regardless of uniform. Call 17 (police) if suspicious.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Bump and Spill Distraction Theft (distraction, severity: moderate). A well-dressed person ‘accidentally’ spills something (coffee, ice cream, sauce) on your clothing. They apologize profusely and begin helping to wipe off the stain, using the commotion to distract you while an accomplice steals your wallet, phone, or bag. Alternatively, a jogger may bump into you hard, knocking you off balance. While helping you recover, they or a partner steal your belongings. Another variation involves someone dropping coins or papers near you — as you helpfully bend down to assist, an accomplice grabs your bag from behind. How to avoid: Immediately check your belongings if anyone spills on or bumps you. Do not let strangers touch your clothing. Step back from anyone getting too close. Keep bags secured and in front of you. Be suspicious of any unusual contact in crowded areas.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Rental Car Break-in / Smash and Grab (accommodation, severity: high). Marseille and the surrounding Provence region are notorious for car break-ins targeting tourists, especially at beaches and the Calanques. Thieves identify rental cars by license plates, sterile interiors, and window stickers. They smash windows and steal bags in seconds, even if you’re only away for a few minutes. Some thieves target cars in traffic — approaching at red lights or in slow traffic to grab items through open windows. One traveler reported their car was completely stripped of belongings after parking near a beach for just 10 minutes. How to avoid: Never leave anything visible in the car — even empty bags look promising to thieves. Remove all rental car identifying stickers if possible. Park in attended lots when available. Never park near the Calanques trailheads with valuables in car. Take all valuables with you. Keep windows closed and doors locked even in traffic. Use the trunk for storage, but load it before arriving at destination.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Vacation Rental / Airbnb Scam (accommodation, severity: high). Scammers create fake vacation rental listings on platforms like Airbnb or independent websites, using stolen photos from legitimate properties. The listing shows an attractive apartment at below-market prices. Victims pay deposits or full rental fees, then arrive to find the property doesn’t exist, belongs to someone else, or is drastically different from the listing. In the ‘bait and switch’ version, the host cancels just before check-in, claiming the original property is unavailable, and offers an inferior substitute. France, including Paris and coastal areas near Marseille, has seen an epidemic of such scams. How to avoid: Book only through established platforms with buyer protection. Never pay outside the platform. Read reviews carefully and check host history. Reverse image search listing photos. If price seems too good to be true, it probably is. Verify the address exists on Google Maps/Street View. Contact host with specific questions about the property.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Beach Theft at Prado Beaches (theft, severity: moderate). While tourists swim or relax with their attention elsewhere, thieves steal unattended belongings from beach towels and bags. The Prado beaches are pleasant during the day but have many shaded areas that provide cover for thieves. At the Calanques, visitors often leave belongings at the beach while swimming, making easy targets. Some thieves work in pairs — one distracts with conversation while the other takes items from nearby spots. How to avoid: Never leave valuables unattended on the beach. Use a waterproof pouch for phone and money while swimming. Take turns watching belongings with travel companions. Leave valuables at your accommodation. Avoid beaches late at night, especially alone. Use beach lockers where available.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — La Mère Poulard Restaurant Price Trap (tourist-trap, severity: high). La Mère Poulard trades on a century of hype for its signature soufflé omelette. Visitors report paying €40–€80 for a basic omelette — often dry, flavorless, and ‘nothing extraordinary.’ A bottle of cider here runs €19–€26, versus under €3 at any supermarket on the mainland. Service is notoriously slow; 30–40 minutes just to get your order taken is typical. How to avoid: Skip dining on the island entirely. If you must eat on-island, check menu prices carefully before sitting. Eat at restaurants in nearby Pontorson or Cancale instead. Bring a picnic lunch to the island.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — Island Restaurant Tourist Trap (tourist-trap, severity: high). Every restaurant on the island gets described as a tourist trap — bad service, mediocre food, prices that nobody who lives nearby would pay. With no repeat customers, the restaurants have no incentive to improve. Visitors report €4.50 for a 500 ml bottle of water, €9.80 for a small beer, €7 per glass of wine, and €3.50 for a mediocre crêpe. How to avoid: Pack your own food and water before arriving. Eat breakfast before visiting and dinner after leaving. Coffee or aperitifs are acceptable for the experience, but avoid full meals. Visit the fishing port of Cancale nearby for excellent seafood at fair prices.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — Overpriced Parking Lot (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). The official parking lot charges inflated prices, with little signage about the cost before you drive in. Visitors report paying €14–€25, including €17 for just 30 minutes in one case and €9.80 for under two hours in a nearly empty lot in another. Once you’ve driven to Mont-Saint-Michel, there is no alternative — and the pricing reflects that. How to avoid: Check current parking rates online before visiting. Budget 15-20 euros for parking in your trip costs. Consider taking public transport or organized tours instead. Arrive early or late to minimize parking time.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — Unlicensed Bay Crossing Danger (safety-hazard, severity: high). The bay around Mont-Saint-Michel contains deadly quicksand pockets and experiences extreme tides that rise at speeds up to 6 km/hour — faster than a person can run. Tourists attempting to cross the bay without certified guides have died or required helicopter rescue after becoming trapped in quicksand as tides rushed in. In 2019 alone, multiple rescues were needed including one helicopter extraction. How to avoid: Do not set foot on the bay without a certified guide from the Préfecture de la Manche — people have died. Book official bay-crossing tours through the tourism office. Check tide schedules before you visit. There are only 67 officially authorized guides; verify credentials before paying.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — Worthless Museum Trap (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Mont-Saint-Michel has several small private museums charging €9 each or €18 for a multi-museum pass. Visitors describe them as dusty and dilapidated, with shabby exhibits crammed into tiny rooms. Three of the four have been called ‘a disgrace,’ with dirt, mold on the walls, and little historical content. They exist to separate tourists from their money. How to avoid: Skip all private museums on the island. The only worthwhile paid attraction is the Abbey itself (13 euros). Read reviews before paying any entrance fee. The free walking experience and architecture are the real attractions.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — Candy Shop Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Several candy shops on the Grande Rue use deceptive pricing. Prices are listed at €8 per 100 grams — roughly double the typical tourist rate of €4. Visitors report paying as much as €31 for a single bag of sweets. Some shops use aggressive sales tactics, pressuring you to pay after you’ve already filled the bag. How to avoid: Ask for total price before filling any bag.
