Calculate the per-gram cost before selecting items. Don’t feel obligated to buy if prices seem excessive. Buy sweets in mainland towns instead.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — Crowded Street Theft (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Mont-Saint-Michel’s single narrow street becomes extremely congested, especially from 10:30am to 5pm in peak season. The crushing crowds create ideal conditions for pickpockets who exploit tourists distracted by sights and jostled by crowds. Items left unattended — including wheelchairs, strollers, and bags at the abbey entrance where they must be left — can easily be stolen. How to avoid: Visit early morning (before 10am) or evening (after 5pm) to avoid worst crowds. Wear crossbody bags in front of your body. Keep valuables in front pockets or money belt. Never leave bags unattended even briefly.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — Parking Lot Vehicle Break-In (theft, severity: moderate). Thieves target vehicles in the Mont-Saint-Michel parking lot, particularly rental cars identifiable by stickers or foreign plates. They watch tourists rearrange luggage in the lot (revealing valuables), then break into cars while owners spend hours visiting the island. This is part of a wider pattern of tourist parking lot thefts across Normandy. How to avoid: Move valuables to the trunk before you arrive, not in the lot where thieves are watching. Don’t rearrange luggage visibly in the parking area. Peel off rental company stickers before you leave the airport. Park in high-traffic areas near the entrance rather than the quieter edges.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — Hotel Overbooking Scam (accommodation, severity: moderate). Hotels on Mont-Saint-Michel (mostly owned by one family/company with monopoly pricing power) have been reported to overbook rooms and then relocate guests to inferior mainland hotels at the last minute. Visitors receive emails about ‘overbooking’ and forced relocation to distant hotels at the same premium price, suspecting they were bumped for higher-paying tour groups. How to avoid: Book well in advance and get written confirmation. Consider staying in mainland hotels intentionally — they offer better value. Book directly with hotels rather than through aggregators. Have backup accommodation options researched.

Scam alert in Mont-Saint-Michel, France — Tide Timing Trap (safety-hazard, severity: moderate). Tourists often plan visits around seeing spectacular high tides but don’t understand tide mechanics. High tides reaching 14 meters can occur, but they don’t happen every day. Conversely, those who don’t check tide schedules may be caught off-guard by rapidly rising water on the causeway or bay areas. The incoming tide can isolate visitors or trap them against walls. How to avoid: Check tide schedules online before visiting (available on tourism website). Understand that exceptional tides only occur a few times yearly. Time your visit for 2 hours before high tide for best experience. Never walk the bay without awareness of tide timing.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — Tram Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Montpellier’s tram is prime hunting ground for organized pickpocket teams. They work during busy periods — boarding, exiting, when passengers are pressed together and distracted. One person creates a distraction or blocks your movement while the others slip hands into bags and pockets. The whole thing takes seconds, and the thief is off at the next stop before you notice anything is gone. How to avoid: Wear bags zipped and close to your body in front. Keep hands on your belongings during boarding and exiting. Avoid placing phones or wallets in back pockets. Stay alert at busy stops like Comédie and Gare Saint-Roch.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — Place de la Comédie Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Place de la Comédie, Montpellier’s grand central square, draws tourists and pickpockets in roughly equal measure. Thieves blend into the crowds around the Three Graces fountain, targeting visitors photographing the square or seated at terrace cafés. Teams work together — one asks directions, the other works the bag or pocket — and the square’s open layout gives them easy exits in every direction. How to avoid: Keep bags on your lap or looped around chair legs at cafés. Be wary of anyone approaching with distractions. Don’t leave phones or wallets on café tables. Stay alert while taking photos.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — Gare Saint-Roch Train Station Theft (theft, severity: high). Gare Saint-Roch is Montpellier’s main station and the city’s most reliable spot for opportunistic luggage theft. Thieves watch for tourists who arrive looking lost or preoccupied — consulting a phone map, fumbling with tickets, wrestling bags — and strike in the handful of seconds it takes you to check a schedule. The short walk between the station and the tram stops is where most incidents happen; the area also turns rougher after dark. How to avoid: Keep luggage in physical contact with you — hand on the handle, strap under a chair leg. Work out your route before you arrive so you’re not reading a map on the concourse. Use bags with locks. Avoid lingering outside the station at night; catch the tram straight out.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — TGV Train Luggage Theft (theft, severity: high). Thieves board TGV trains during brief station stops, posing as passengers. They position themselves with views of the luggage racks and wait for any distraction. Working in teams, one person engages the victim in conversation while the other grabs luggage from the rack and exits just before the doors close. With up to 400 such incidents monthly on French trains, this is a well-organized crime. How to avoid: Keep valuables and essentials in a small bag you keep with you. Use cable locks to secure luggage to racks. Sit where you can see your luggage. Stay alert during station stops.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — Fake Petition / Deaf Charity Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Scammers approach tourists with clipboards, often pretending to be deaf-mute and collecting signatures for a fake charity. The petition is typically written in English to target foreign visitors. While you’re distracted reading or signing, accomplices pickpocket you. If you sign, they demand a donation and can become aggressive when refused. The petition itself is worthless and no charity ever receives any funds. How to avoid: Firmly say ‘Non merci’ and keep walking without slowing down. Never sign anything on the street. Don’t engage in conversation. Keep hands on your belongings when approached.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — Gold Ring Scam (street-scam, severity: moderate). A stranger bends down near you and picks up what appears to be a gold ring, asking if you dropped it. When you say no, they examine it and claim it’s marked ’18k gold’ and must be valuable. They offer to sell it for a fraction of its supposed worth, or guilt you into giving them a ‘finder’s fee.’ The ring is worthless brass, and while you’re engaged, an accomplice may be pickpocketing you. How to avoid: Simply say ‘no’ and walk away without engaging. Don’t examine or touch the ring. Keep moving and maintain awareness of your surroundings. Be aware that accomplices may be nearby.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — Taxi Overcharging / Broken Meter Scam (transport, severity: moderate). Some taxi drivers target tourists by claiming the meter is broken and quoting inflated flat rates, taking unnecessarily long routes, or failing to reset the meter to the base fare before starting. The airport to city center trip should cost approximately 35 euros during the day and 42 euros at night, but unsuspecting tourists may pay significantly more. Drivers may also refuse to provide receipts. How to avoid: Know approximate fares before traveling (airport to center: ~35 euros day, ~42 euros night). Insist on using the meter and verify it starts at 2 euros. Track your route on Google Maps. Use official taxi stands or ride-hailing apps.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — Restaurant Bill Padding (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Some restaurants in tourist areas inflate bills with hidden charges or serve items not ordered. Common tactics include automatically bringing expensive bottled water instead of offering free tap water, adding cover charges not mentioned on menus, or ‘accidentally’ adding extra items to the bill. Tourists who don’t check bills carefully pay significantly more than they should. How to avoid: Always request ‘une carafe d’eau’ for free tap water. Check menu prices before ordering. Review your bill carefully before paying. Know that service is included — tipping beyond rounding up is optional.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — Rental Car Break-In (theft, severity: high). Southern France has high rates of car break-ins, and rental cars are prime targets. Thieves identify rentals by company stickers, foreign plates, or luggage visible inside. They stake out tourist sites, knowing how long visitors typically stay, then break windows to steal bags and valuables. Rest stops along the A9 motorway approaching Montpellier are particularly notorious. How to avoid: Never leave any belongings visible in the car — even empty bags look promising. Store items in the trunk before arriving at destinations. Remove or cover rental company stickers if possible. Use attended underground parking.

Scam alert in Montpellier, France — ATM Skimming (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). Criminals install skimming devices on ATMs that capture your card data and PIN. These devices are designed to look like part of the machine and are difficult to detect. Tourist areas are targeted because they process many foreign cards and victims are less familiar with how local ATMs should look. Your card details are then used to create clones or make fraudulent purchases. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside bank branches during business hours. Wiggle the card slot and keypad before inserting your card. Cover the keypad with your hand when entering your PIN. Monitor your account for unauthorized transactions.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Beach Grab / Swim-and-Steal (theft, severity: high). You wade into the Mediterranean off Promenade des Anglais for a quick swim, leaving your bag on the pebbles. Minutes later, someone who has been watching from a bench a hundred meters away walks past, scoops up the bag, and is gone before you dry off. The private beach clubs are no safer — thieves pay the entry fee and work the loungers while paying customers sleep. How to avoid: Take only what you can hold in a waterproof pouch into the water. Leave passport, cards, and phone in your hotel safe. If you sunbathe, use your bag as a pillow rather than leaving it on top of your towel. Travel with a companion and swim in shifts so someone is always watching the gear.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Taxi Meter Manipulation / Overcharging (transport, severity: high). Nice taxi drivers have a long-running reputation for working tourists over at the airport and train station. Drivers claim the meter is broken, quote inflated flat rates, cover the meter with a hand, or take the long route through Promenade des Anglais traffic. Many refuse credit cards and skip the legally required receipt. Official fixed rates: airport to Nice center €32, airport to Cannes €85, airport to Monaco €95. How to avoid: Know the fixed rates before you land. Confirm the price before you get in, and insist on the meter for any non-fixed route. Use Uber or Bolt when you want tracked, transparent pricing. Ask for a receipt every time — drivers who refuse are the ones worth reporting.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Airport Tram Ticket Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). The ticket machines at Nice Airport sell only a special ‘airport ticket’ priced at €10 round trip — roughly three times the regular tram fare of €1.70. The machines don’t advertise the cheaper option, and most tourists pay the premium because they don’t know one exists. How to avoid: Walk one stop to Grand Arenas, where the machines sell the regular €1.70 fare. Better still, buy on the Lignes d’Azur mobile app before you even leave the terminal. The tram is the same; only the ticket costs six times more if you buy it where the tourists do.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Gold Ring Scam (distraction, severity: moderate). A stranger bends down near you along Promenade des Anglais, picks up what looks like a gold ring, and asks if you dropped it. When you say no, they show you the ’14k’ stamp and insist it must be valuable. They offer to sell it for a fraction of its ‘worth,’ or press it into your hand and demand a finder’s fee. The ring is brass worth pennies — and while you’re engaging, an accomplice is often working your pockets. How to avoid: Say *non* and keep walking without slowing down. Do not touch the ring — the moment you hold it, they pivot to pressure. Keep hands on your bag or in your pockets. Scan for the second player: ring scams almost always run with an accomplice.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Petition / Deaf Charity Scam (distraction, severity: high). A young woman approaches along Promenade des Anglais with a clipboard, points to her ears and mouth to signal deaf-mute, and asks whether you speak English. She wants a signature for a ‘deaf children’s charity.’ While you’re reading the clipboard, an accomplice works your bag from behind. If you sign, she flips to a donation column showing €20 and €50 contributions and becomes loud if you refuse. The charity does not exist. How to avoid: Say *non merci* firmly and keep moving. Do not stop to read anything handed to you on the street — legitimate French charities do not solicit signatures from strangers. If you’re already holding the clipboard, hand it back and walk on without engaging.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Bird Droppings / Mustard Scam (street-scam, severity: high). Something warm and wet lands on your shoulder from behind — it looks like bird droppings, or maybe squirted mustard. Within seconds, a friendly stranger materializes with tissues, tutting about the pigeons and offering to help you clean up. While you set down your bag and shrug off your jacket, their accomplice empties your pockets. The ‘droppings’ are usually paste or sauce sprayed from a concealed bottle. How to avoid: If anything unexpectedly lands on you, step back from any ‘helper’ and say *non merci, ça va*. Walk into the nearest café or shop to clean up on your own. Do not set your bag down; do not take off a jacket that holds your wallet or phone. Treat the helpful stranger as part of the setup, not a coincidence.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Vol à la Portière (Car Door Grab) (theft, severity: high). Thieves along the Riviera watch for rental cars — easy to spot by their stickers and foreign plates — and strike when you’re stopped at a red light or parked at a scenic turnout. They yank the passenger door open, grab whatever’s on the seat (phone on a mount, handbag, camera), and are gone on a scooter before the light changes. The French call this *vol à la portière*, and it happens fast. How to avoid: Lock all doors the moment you sit down — many rentals don’t auto-lock. Keep windows up at lights and stow bags and phones on the floor behind the front seats, not on the passenger seat. Peel off the rental agency stickers where you can. Keep more space than feels natural from the car ahead so you have room to maneuver.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Rental Car Break-In (accommodation, severity: high). Thieves stake out parking lots at scenic viewpoints and beach access roads, watching for rental cars by their stickers and foreign plates. They know roughly how long the average visitor spends at each attraction, so they wait for you to walk away, smash a window, and pull out whatever’s in the trunk in under a minute. France has one of the highest rates of tourist car break-ins in Western Europe. How to avoid: Do not leave anything visible in the car, not even empty bags — a thief doesn’t know they’re empty. Load the trunk before you arrive, not in the lot where the thief is watching. Clear out maps, guidebooks, and rental paperwork that mark you as a visitor. Use attended parking garages when the choice is available.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Fake Police Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Two men in plain clothes flash what look like police badges and tell you they need to check your wallet for counterfeit bills. Sometimes a ‘lost tourist’ accomplice has just asked you to break a large note, and the ‘officer’ arrives seconds later claiming street currency exchange is illegal. While one inspects your documents, the other palms cash from your wallet. Real French police do not check tourists’ wallets on the street. How to avoid: Real officers will only ask to see ID, never the wallet itself. Ask clearly to see their *carte de police* — the photo ID card with badge number — and offer to walk to the nearest *commissariat* together. Genuine police will comply; scammers won’t. Never hand over your wallet on the street, and dial 17 if something feels off.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Restaurant Overcharging / Water Scam (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Restaurants along Promenade des Anglais and in Vieux Nice run a familiar playbook on tourists. Waiters bring expensive bottled water when you ask for *eau*, bills include items you didn’t order, and the English menu carries higher prices than the French one. Some waiters push for ‘American-style’ tips even though service is already included, and a few refuse to seat solo diners for anything less than a full multi-course meal. How to avoid: Say *une carafe d’eau, s’il vous plaît* — tap water is free by law. Ask for the French menu and compare prices line by line. Check the bill against what you ordered before paying. *Service compris* means service is already included; any additional ‘service charge’ line is not owed.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Public Transport Ticket Fine Trap (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). You buy a tram or bus ticket, board, and assume you’re done. You’re not. Every ticket must be validated in the small yellow or orange machine on board — and inspectors issue €40 on-the-spot fines to anyone holding an unvalidated ticket, bought or otherwise. Drivers rarely warn about it, so tourists get caught every day. How to avoid: Tap your ticket against the validator the instant you board and listen for the confirmation beep. Watch what local passengers do — the machine is small and easy to miss. If you’re not sure, ask the driver directly.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Grand Arenas Tram Stop Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Grand Arenas is the stop savvy travelers use to dodge the €10 airport tram ticket — and the pickpockets know it. Teams (often teenage girls) loiter near the machines watching for tired, luggage-laden visitors. One person offers to ‘help’ you work the machine in broken English, while her partner works the other side of your bag. By the time your €1.70 ticket prints, your phone or wallet is on the far side of the platform. How to avoid: Decline all offers of help at the machines with a firm *non merci*. Keep luggage in front of you, one hand on the handle and one on your bag. If you’re traveling solo, ignore anyone who approaches while you’re at the screen. The machine is simple — English is a button on the first screen.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Rose / Flower Seller Scam (distraction, severity: low). Men with bundles of roses work the restaurant terraces along Vieux Nice, offering a ‘free’ flower for the lady. The moment either of you touches or accepts it, the price jumps to €10–€20, and they lean on the social pressure of a romantic dinner to get paid. Some sellers circle back repeatedly during the meal, betting on you paying just to make them go away. How to avoid: Say *non merci* before the rose is on the table. Do not touch it — the transaction begins the moment you do. If it’s been placed down, leave it where it is and keep ignoring the seller. Ask restaurant staff to step in if he doesn’t move along. Indoor seating avoids the whole thing.

Scam alert in Nice, France — ATM Skimming (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). Criminals fit hidden card readers and fake keypads over ATM slots to capture your card data and PIN. A common variant uses a false insert that jams your card inside — when you leave to find help, the scammer returns, retrieves the card, and now has both the plastic and the code. Standalone ATMs on tourist streets are the usual targets. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside bank branches during business hours where tampering is less likely. Wiggle the card slot before inserting — skimmers tend to be loosely attached. Cover the keypad completely when entering your PIN. If your card gets stuck, do not leave the machine; call the bank number printed on it immediately. Enable transaction alerts on all travel cards before you leave home.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Luxury Watch Theft (theft, severity: high). The Riviera has seen a sharp rise in thefts targeting Rolex, Patek, and Audemars Piguet wearers. Spotters cruise La Croisette equivalents and luxury hotel terraces identifying marks, then signal to riders on scooters with tampered plates who pull alongside and wrench the watch off the wrist. Others work on foot in crowded areas. The attacks can be quick, and they can turn violent if you resist. How to avoid: Leave high-value watches at home or in the hotel safe — anything over €5,000 is a target on the Riviera in summer. If you must wear one, keep it under a long sleeve. Skip the conspicuous jewelry at beach clubs and on restaurant terraces, and sit with your back to a wall so no one can approach from behind. Confirm your travel insurance covers jewelry up to the item’s value before you leave home.

Scam alert in Nice, France — Vacation Rental Scam (accommodation, severity: high). Scammers post fake listings on Airbnb, Vrbo, and independent rental sites, using photos stolen from real apartments and pricing them just below market to hook quick bookings. Once you wire a deposit outside the platform, the listing vanishes — and when you arrive, the address is a parking garage, the apartment belongs to someone else, or the building doesn’t exist. The Riviera sees a wave of these every summer. How to avoid: Book only on the official platform and keep all payments on it — that is the only recourse you have. A wire transfer outside Airbnb is a gift you will not get back. Reverse-image-search the photos before booking. Read reviews for specific, verifiable details about the apartment, not generic praise. If the price is noticeably below comparable listings, assume it’s fake.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Gold Ring Trick (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). You're walking along the Seine near the Pont des Arts when a woman ten paces ahead of you bends down and theatrically lifts a gleaming gold ring off the pavement. "Excusez-moi, monsieur — is this yours?" Before you can respond she's already turning the ring over in the light, examining the inside, and shaking her head: "Too big for my finger. You take it — finder's luck." The ring goes into your palm.

She holds eye contact, smiles. Then the script flips. There's a sick child at home, or her husband lost his job last week, or she's behind on rent — could you spare a few euros? She gestures at the ring still in your hand: you're so lucky, you have a real gold ring, surely you can give back. If you try to return it, she steps back, hands raised — it's yours now, she says. If you walk away, she follows. If you raise your voice, two more people materialize at the edge of your vision. They were the next "finders."

The ring is brass plated to look like 18-carat gold; the operator buys them by the bag for under €1 each. The whole scam runs on a forced-gift reciprocity loop — once you've held it, she can frame any refusal as ungrateful. Euro for Visitors has documented this exact play running on the Pont des Arts continuously since the early 2000s, and the same operators rotate between Champ de Mars, the Tuileries, and the Louvre Quai. Keep your hands in your pockets when anyone bends down ahead of you near the Seine bridges — refusing the ring is the whole defense. How to avoid: Say 'Non, merci' and keep walking without slowing down Never touch or accept the ring — the moment you hold it, you're obligated in their script Ignore anyone who bends down dramatically in front of you near tourist sites If they follow you, walk toward a group of people or a nearby shop Know that legitimate lost-and-found goes to the police, not random strangers

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Sacré-Cœur Friendship Bracelet Trap (distraction, severity: high). You start the climb up the famous white steps toward Sacré-Cœur and a man at the bottom calls out: "From America? England? Welcome, my friend!" His hand is on your wrist before the greeting finishes. He's already started looping a colored thread around your fingers — a friendship bracelet, a souvenir, free, just for fun. The weaving moves fast. It's almost hypnotic. You haven't said a word.

The bracelet is tied. The smile changes. "€10. €20. €30 for the better one — the gold one." If you reach for scissors to cut it off, his hand stops yours. If you turn to walk up the steps, two of his crew step into the gap on the stair above you. You can't go down without passing the man you started with. You can't go up without passing his friends. In 2014, Paris Police Commissioner Bernard Boucault was personally slapped by bracelet operators on these same steps when he tried to intervene; his chauffeur was punched and the head of public safety was kicked.

The whole hustle hinges on the wrist grab. Once the thread is tied around your fingers, you can't simply hand it back — and that's the mechanism that converts a sidewalk encounter into a payment demand. Sacré-Cœur draws roughly 10 million visitors a year, which is why the same crews work these steps every daylight hour. Keep both hands in pockets or holding a phone or bag strap as you climb — and the moment anyone reaches for your wrist, pull back hard and shout "NON!" before they make contact. The Montmartre funicular bypasses the steps entirely and costs one Métro ticket. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets or hold something (phone, bag strap) as you climb the Sacré-Cœur steps. Say a firm *non* and pull your arm back the instant someone reaches for your wrist — do not let them make contact. Do not engage or make eye contact; looking away while walking is your best defense. If cornered, loudly say ‘Appelez la police!’ (Call the police) — they scatter the moment attention is drawn. Visit Sacré-Cœur very early morning (before 8am) when the scammers haven’t set up yet. Take the Montmartre funicular instead of the steps to avoid the gauntlet entirely. If a bracelet gets tied, refuse to pay and walk to the police officers stationed near Place du Tertre.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Deaf-Mute Petition Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: high). You step off the RER at Champ de Mars or out of the Louvre courtyard and a young woman intercepts you with a clipboard and an earnest expression. She points to her ears, then her mouth — deaf and mute — and gestures for you to sign. The clipboard's top sheet is a petition: "Stop the abuse of disabled children" or "Help fund autism research in France." The cause sounds real. You sign.

The pen is barely back in her hand when she flips the clipboard to a second page — a donation column with €10, €20, €50 already filled in by previous "signers" in different handwriting. She points insistently at the highest amount. Behind you, while your eyes were on the petition, an accomplice has already worked your back pocket. They're walking away by the time the clipboard turns. If you refuse to donate, she follows you, pointing at the page. The phone is already gone.

The clipboard is the distraction; the lift is the actual scam. Real French deaf advocacy organizations — like the Fédération Nationale des Sourds de France — do not solicit on the street. Aéroport de Paris workers who tried to warn tourists at CDG have been physically attacked by these crews; they operate in shifts of 6–10 people across every major tourist corridor in Paris, with the Eiffel Tower south entrance, the Louvre pyramid, and the Opéra Garnier steps as the highest-density zones. Never sign anything from a stranger on the street in Paris — keep your phone in a front zipped pocket and walk past clipboards without breaking stride. How to avoid: Never sign anything from a stranger on the street in Paris — legitimate charities do not operate this way. Shake your head firmly, say ‘Non,’ and walk without breaking stride. If they block your path, step around them without engaging — say nothing. Be especially alert near the Eiffel Tower south entrance and Louvre courtyards. Keep your phone in a front zipped pocket, not a back pocket or loose bag. Travel with a companion and watch each other’s bags when anyone approaches. Real French deaf organizations (like the Fédération Nationale des Sourds de France) do not solicit on the street.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Boarding-Crush Wallet Lift (pickpocket, severity: high). It's rush hour at Châtelet–Les Halles and the Line 4 train pulls in already full. You squeeze on. The departure chime sounds. As the doors begin to close, three teenagers shove their way in — a hard, deliberate jostle that presses everyone in the car together for two or three seconds. You take the bump, find a strap to hold, and move on with your day.

At your stop, you reach for your phone. Empty pocket. Or your wallet is gone from the inside of your jacket. The push from the front was the distraction — one of the group pinned your attention to the door area while another worked your pockets from behind. They got off at the next station, two minutes after they got on. You're now a station and a half away with no phone and no idea which of the dozen people in that crush did it.

A 2016 investigation found that a single organized gang was responsible for two-thirds of all Paris Métro thefts, employing roughly 100 girls recruited from Eastern Europe with daily theft quotas of €300–€1,000. Paris generates more pickpocket-related travel reports than any other city worldwide — about 283 thefts per million tourists per year — and the RER B from CDG to central Paris is the single highest-risk corridor in the system. If a group rushes the doors right at the closing chime, let them have the car and wait for the next train; valuables go in front-zipped pockets or a money belt, never an outer jacket pocket or back pocket. How to avoid: Keep valuables in a front zipped pocket, money belt, or inside jacket pocket — never outer or back pockets. Hold your bag in front of you on crowded trains, not slung to the side or back. If a group rushes the doors right at closing, let them pass and wait for the next train. Be extra vigilant at Châtelet, Gare du Nord, Opéra, and on RER B from CDG Airport. Consider a slim RFID-blocking wallet inside a shirt pocket for passport and cards. Keep one hand on your bag or pocket in crowded cars. Board train cars near the driver’s compartment where CCTV coverage is better.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Fake Police Officer Wallet Check (impersonation, severity: high). You're walking back to your hotel in Pigalle or down a side street near Opéra after dinner when two men step out of a doorway and flash a folded ID at you. "Police. Standard drug check, monsieur — passport and wallet, please." Their French is fluent, their suits are neat, the IDs look official. They aren't standing near a marked car or a uniformed officer, but it's late and you're tired and being detained by French police feels worse than complying.

One officer takes your passport and starts examining it slowly, asking where you're staying, when you arrived. The other asks to see your wallet — they need to verify you aren't carrying counterfeit euros, a fraud problem on the rise in this neighborhood. Your eyes follow the passport. You don't see the second officer fan through your bills. By the time they hand everything back with a polite "merci, bonne soirée," your wallet is €200 lighter, or your card has been swapped for a near-identical decoy.

Real Police Nationale officers operating in plain clothes do not stop tourists for random passport or cash inspections without a uniformed colleague present, and they will never ask to handle your money. The Bonjour Guide and multiple French consumer-protection sites document this scam running primarily in Pigalle, around Moulin Rouge, the backstreets near Opéra, and the Gare du Nord exits after dark. Demand to be taken to the nearest commissariat to continue any "check" — real officers will comply, scammers will dissolve into the street. If you feel pressured, dial 17 (Police Nationale) on the spot. How to avoid: Ask to be taken to the nearest commissariat (police station) — real officers will comply; scammers won’t. Request a uniformed officer be present before showing any document. Keep your passport in your hotel safe and carry a photocopy plus your driver’s license instead. Never open your wallet or show cash to anyone claiming to be police on the street. Call 17 (French emergency police line) immediately if you feel unsafe. Real French police carry a carte de police (police card) with photo, name, and badge number — ask to see it clearly. Walk toward a busy public area or shop if you feel threatened.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Tourist-Zone Restaurant Overcharge (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). The café two blocks from Notre-Dame has a chalkboard out front: croque-monsieur €8, jambon-beurre €7, café €2.50. The prices are normal for Paris. You sit down at a sidewalk table. The waiter brings a basket of bread, a small carafe-shaped bottle of water, and a paper menu in English. You order the croque-monsieur and a Coke.

The bill is €34. There's a €5 "couvert" cover charge, €7 for the bottled water you assumed was tap, the Coke is €9.50 instead of the €4 you'd expected, and the croque-monsieur is now €15 because it turns out the chalkboard prices were the lunch menu, which ended at 14h30. The waiter shrugs at the chalkboard outside: "Carte du soir, monsieur." Service compris is included by law, but a 12% tip line is also pre-printed on the receipt.

In July 2025, Le Parisien ran a sting where two journalists ordered identical lunches at Eiffel Tower-adjacent restaurants — one dressed as a Parisian local, one as an American tourist in an Eiffel Tower t-shirt and baseball cap. The American was charged about 50% more across every restaurant tested: bigger Coke for €9.50 vs the local's small Coke for €6.50, charged bottled water vs free tap, a tip line that the waiter physically obscured on the card terminal. French law requires identical pricing regardless of language or nationality — charging tourists more is fraud. Ask "L'eau du robinet, s'il vous plaît" (tap water) the moment you sit, "C'est offert?" (is this free?) for anything that arrives unrequested, and walk two streets away from any monument before you sit down to eat. How to avoid: Ask ‘L’eau du robinet, s’il vous plaît’ (tap water, please) immediately — it’s free and legally required. Clarify ‘C’est offert?’ (Is this free?) when bread, olives, or nibbles are brought to the table. Check the full indoor menu and prices before sitting down. Walk 2-3 streets away from major monuments for better prices and authenticity. Check Google Maps reviews filtered by locals — 3.5 stars with 2000+ reviews often beats a polished tourist trap. Service charge (service compris) is legally included in all French restaurant prices — additional ‘service charge’ on the bill is fraudulent. Pay attention when entering your card PIN — some waiters try to change the tip amount.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Trocadéro Three-Card Monte (street-scam, severity: moderate). A folding table sets up across the plaza at Trocadéro with the Eiffel Tower as the backdrop. A dealer with quick hands moves three plastic cups around a small ball — the audience can see the ball, can almost track it. A tourist in the crowd lays down €50 on the cup that looks obvious. The dealer lifts it: ball. The crowd cheers. The dealer hands over €100. The "winner" walks off counting the cash.

You step closer. The next round you swear you can see the ball under the left cup the entire time — the dealer's hand is too slow, you've got this. You put down €20. The cup lifts. Empty. Try again? €40 doubles your chance. You lose. The dealer is already restarting; the lookout at the edge of the crowd is watching the path from the Métro for police. The crowd that was cheering you on a minute ago has shifted to the next mark.

The "winner" you saw was a shill on the dealer's payroll; the cheering audience was salted with three or four more accomplices; the lookouts collapse the table and scatter the moment any uniformed officer turns toward Trocadéro. The game is mathematically and physically rigged — the dealer palms the ball during the shuffle so it isn't under any cup when you bet. In August 2025, a TikTok of American tourist Nathalia Duques crying after losing "so much money" at the Eiffel Tower three-card monte hit 11 million views, and the comments were merciless: "Imagine being scammed by 3 cups in 2025." The game is unwinnable — even watching marks you as a target. Walk past without slowing down. How to avoid: Never bet on street gambling — the game is mathematically and physically rigged; you cannot win. The ‘winners’ are part of the crew — their job is to make you think winning is possible. Walk past without stopping or watching — even spectating marks you as a potential target. If you’ve lost money, walk away immediately — trying to ‘win it back’ will only cost more. Report the location to police, but know that arrests are rare because operators move constantly. The sleight of hand is professional-grade — even knowing the trick, you cannot beat it.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The CDG Airport Unlicensed Taxi Ambush (transport, severity: high). You walk out of CDG arrivals after a transatlantic flight, dazed and dragging two suitcases. A polished man in a dark suit steps over with a clipboard and a confident smile. "Taxi to Paris? €70, no traffic problem, very fast." Outside, the official taxi queue is twenty deep with a 30-minute wait. €70 sounds reasonable. You follow him through the door. The car is a black sedan with no roof sign, no meter, and no "TAXI PARISIEN" markings.

At your hotel he hands you a printed bill: €200. There's a €40 "airport surcharge," €30 for tolls he claims he paid (CDG has none on the relevant route), €20 per piece of luggage, and a €20 "evening supplement" that doesn't exist. When you protest, he locks the doors and explains, calmly, that you agreed to €70 plus extras. With your bags in his trunk and the hotel doorman already moving on to the next guest, you hand over the card.

Paris taxi regulation sets a fixed flat rate from CDG: €56 to the Right Bank, €65 to the Left Bank, no exceptions, no extras, posted on signs at the official rank. Unlicensed operators exploit the seam between baggage claim and the legitimate queue — they cannot legally solicit inside the terminal, but they do anyway. One traveler documented being charged €200 for a trip that should cost €56; another was quoted €90 inside, then told it would be €120 on arrival. Only take a taxi from the lit "TAXI PARISIEN" rank outside baggage claim — if you're approached inside the terminal, say "Non merci" and walk past. The RER B train to central Paris costs €11.80 and runs every 10 minutes. How to avoid: Only take taxis from the official queue outside baggage claim — look for the illuminated ‘TAXI PARISIEN’ roof sign. Know the official fixed rates: CDG to Right Bank €56, CDG to Left Bank €65, Orly to Paris €40-45. Use the G7 app or Uber/Bolt for pre-priced, tracked rides with driver ratings. If someone approaches inside the terminal, say ‘Non merci’ and walk to the official taxi stand. The RER B train from CDG to central Paris costs €11.80 and takes 35 minutes — the cheapest legitimate option. If a driver changes the price upon arrival, photograph their face and vehicle, refuse to pay the excess, and call 17. Official Paris taxis must run the meter for all rides except fixed airport routes.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Gare du Nord Station Gauntlet (street-scam, severity: high). The Eurostar pulls into Gare du Nord and you walk into Europe's busiest train station hauling two suitcases. You haven't found the Métro signs yet. A man in a semi-official-looking vest steps over: "Tickets? I help, machines are broken today." Behind him, a young woman holds out her phone — could you take her photo by the departures board? Behind her, someone bumps the side of your wheeled bag with an "oh, pardon."

While you're working out the man with the vest, the photo request is positioning you in a corner where the security cameras don't see, and the bag-bumper is testing whether your suitcase handle is in your hand or against your leg. The vest man wants €20 cash for tickets you could buy at the SNCF machine for €2.15. The photo request ends with your camera in someone else's pocket. The luggage bump ends with your laptop bag thirty feet behind you and walking the other direction.

Gare du Nord is the most-reported theft location in Paris because its chaotic confluence of Eurostar, Thalys, RER, Métro, and bus connections gives organized crews perfect cover — the same teams work the main hall through the Eurostar arrival peak hours every day. Police presence is real but pickpockets are skilled at staying just outside an officer's eyeline. Walk straight from your train to the official Métro/RER entrance or the lit taxi rank without stopping in the main hall — buy tickets only from machines (English-language option built in) or the SNCF counter, never from someone who approaches you. How to avoid: Buy tickets from official machines (they have English option) or the SNCF/RATP counter — never from helpful strangers. Keep rolling luggage handle in hand and bag straps across body at all times. Walk with purpose directly to the metro/RER entrance or taxi queue — don’t stop in the main hall. If someone approaches, say ‘Non merci’ and keep walking without engaging. Unofficial taxis congregate outside Eurostar exits — walk past them to the official taxi rank. Know your connection before arriving — check the RATP app for metro directions. The station has police presence, but pickpockets are skilled at avoiding detection.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Phone Snatch Through Closing Doors (theft, severity: high). You're on the Line 1 platform at Châtelet, then on the train standing near the doors, then thirty seconds from your stop — phone in hand, scrolling Google Maps for the walk to your hotel. The doors at République open. People shuffle on and off. The departure chime starts. You glance up.

A hand from the platform side reaches through the closing door, snatches the phone out of your fingers, and is gone before you can register that it happened. The doors finish closing. The train pulls away. You're now en route to Bastille with no phone, no maps, and no way to call your bank or your spouse. By the time you exit at the next station, the thief is back on the Line 1 platform working the next car.

This is the most common phone-theft method in Paris — perfectly timed to the door-closing sequence so victims have no chance to react or pursue. A 2025 variant cuts neck-lanyards in crowded cars, where tourists who think a phone-on-a-string is safer have made themselves easier targets. Métro phone theft is now the number-one petty crime in Paris, concentrated at Châtelet, République, Gare de Lyon, and Bastille. Step away from the door area before you check your phone — stand against a wall or pole with your back covered, or wait until you're seated. Enable Find My iPhone or Google Find My Device with remote-wipe before your trip. How to avoid: Never use your phone near metro doors — step away from the door area when checking maps or messages. Keep your phone in a zipped front pocket, not in hand or dangling from a lanyard, especially when standing. If you must check your phone, turn your back to a wall or pole so no one can approach from behind. Be extra vigilant when the door-closing chime sounds — this is prime snatch time. Enable Find My iPhone/Google Find My Device and remote wipe before your trip. Consider a reinforced phone case with wrist loop (not neck lanyard) for secure grip. Sit rather than stand when possible, keeping the phone on your lap or in a closed bag.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The ATM Distraction & Skim (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). You walk up to a standalone ATM half a block off the Champs-Élysées because the bank queues are long and the standalone says "International Cards Welcome." The slot looks normal. You insert your card and start the withdrawal. Behind you, a man in a windbreaker approaches with a smile and a €20 note in his hand: "Excuse me, monsieur, you dropped this."

You half-turn. Your PIN goes into the keypad while your eyes are on him. His partner across the plaza — phone raised like a tourist photo — has just captured your four digits. The €20 he's holding was always his. While you thank him and turn back, your card is already being swapped for a near-identical decoy by a third person who came up on your other side. You finish the withdrawal, take the cash and the wrong card, and walk away. By the time your bank flags the cloned-card transactions in Marseille that night, you're €4,000 in.

A March 2025 DailyMail report estimated 1 in 10 tourists to France — 212,000 people across five years — had been scammed, with ATM fraud a significant contributor. The highest-risk machines are private/non-bank ATMs near tourist sites, especially in dimly lit doorways or recessed alcoves. Paris also sees periodic skimming hardware attached to legitimate-looking machines around the Champs-Élysées, the Marais, and Montmartre. Use ATMs inside major French bank branches (BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole, Société Générale, LCL) during business hours, cover the keypad with your free hand on every PIN entry, and wiggle the card slot before inserting — skimmers are usually loosely attached. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours — these are monitored and maintained. Cover the keypad completely with your other hand when entering your PIN. Before inserting your card, wiggle the card slot and keypad — skimmers are often loosely attached. Ignore anyone who approaches you mid-transaction — complete or cancel immediately. Use contactless payment wherever possible to reduce ATM usage. Enable transaction alerts on your banking app for immediate fraud detection. Avoid private/independent ATMs in tourist areas — stick to major French banks (BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole, Société Générale).

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Rose Seller Restaurant Shakedown (distraction, severity: low). You're at an outdoor terrace in Le Marais on a summer evening with your partner — bottle of wine half-drunk, the steak just arrived. A man with a basket of roses works the row of tables. He stops at yours: "Pour la belle dame?" Before either of you responds, he's set a single red rose on the table next to your partner's wine glass and stepped back to admire it.

He smiles at you. "€15 for the lady. You take it." If you say no, his expression hardens; he reaches across the table for the rose he placed and refuses to take it back — it's been touched, it's yours. If you push it across the table at him he raises his voice. The four diners at the next table are watching. Your partner is mortified. You hand him a €10 to end it. Forty minutes later, when the dessert arrives, he's back at your table with the same rose and the same line.

The shakedown runs on the social cost of a scene at dinner: the rose itself costs the operator a few centimes, but the public confrontation in front of your partner and other diners is what gets paid. Some operators rotate through the same restaurant strip three or four times an evening, knowing tourists who paid once are easier to bill again. Refuse before the rose touches the table — say "Non, merci, partez" firmly, do not let it land, do not touch it. Indoor seating eliminates the issue entirely; sellers don't enter restaurants. How to avoid: Say ‘Non merci’ firmly before the rose is placed down — don’t let them put it on the table. Do not touch the rose — once you’ve touched it, they’ll claim you’ve ‘accepted’ it. If a rose is placed down unwanted, leave it on the table and continue ignoring the seller. Request restaurant staff intervene if the seller becomes aggressive. Indoor seating eliminates the issue entirely — sellers don’t enter restaurants. A firm, repeated ‘Non’ without further engagement usually ends the interaction.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The Fake Airbnb Phantom Listing (accommodation, severity: high). You're searching Airbnb for a Paris flat. A 2-bedroom in the Marais comes up at €100/night — half the price of comparable listings, with sunny photos of a stone-walled apartment and twenty 5-star reviews. You message the host. He replies fast and friendly: he can offer 15% off if you pay him directly via bank transfer, since "Airbnb takes a huge cut." You wire €700 for a week.

You land at CDG, take the RER B in, and roll your bags up to the address he sent. There's no apartment 4B at that building — the building has three floors. The host's WhatsApp number is disconnected. The Airbnb listing is gone. Airbnb's support, when you finally reach a human, says they cannot help you: the transaction happened outside their platform, so their guarantee doesn't apply. You're now in Paris at 9 p.m. with luggage and no place to sleep.

During the 2024 Paris Olympics, Airbnb removed 59,000 fake listings as the city saw an epidemic of phantom-rental fraud — multiple tourists landed for the Games to find their "confirmed" bookings were never real, leaving them homeless during the world's biggest sporting event. The pattern is consistent: a too-good price, a host who pushes off-platform payment, an address that doesn't quite resolve on Google Street View. The only protection is to keep the entire booking and payment inside Airbnb's platform — a host who asks for a bank transfer for a "discount" is the entire scam. How to avoid: Never pay outside Airbnb’s platform — the only protection is their payment system. Verify the exact address exists using Google Street View before booking. Read reviews carefully and look for specific details about the apartment, not generic praise. Reverse image search listing photos to check if they appear elsewhere. Book with Superhosts who have long track records and many detailed reviews. If a deal seems too good to be true for central Paris, it is. Report suspicious listings to Airbnb immediately.

Scam alert in Paris, France — The 'Clumsy Jogger' Bump-and-Lift (street-scam, severity: moderate). You're on a wide path through the Jardin des Tuileries, mid-morning, with plenty of room for two pedestrians to pass. A man in running gear angles toward you and bumps shoulder-to-shoulder. "Pardon, monsieur, pardon — are you okay?" He rests a hand on your jacket near the chest pocket, brushes the sleeve, checks if anything fell. The contact lasts maybe three seconds. He's already jogging again. "Désolé, désolé."

You take a few more steps along the path before reaching for your phone to check directions. Empty pocket. The "clumsy jogger" lifted it during the apology — his palm on your jacket near the chest pocket was the slip, his fast departure was the cover. By the time you realize, he's two hundred meters away and turning into the Place de la Concorde crowd.

This is a classic distraction lift: the unexpected physical contact masks the hand work, and the over-the-top apology buys two or three seconds before you think to check your pockets. Variants include someone "accidentally" spilling coffee on you and helping clean it up, dropping a heavy map at your feet to make you bend down, or asking elaborate directions while a partner approaches your blind side. The Tuileries, the Luxembourg Gardens, and the Seine quaysides are the highest-density zones because joggers and tourists mix naturally. If anyone bumps you in a public space, immediately check every pocket while keeping your eyes on the person — never let a stranger touch your clothing to "help" with anything. How to avoid: If bumped, immediately check your pockets and bag while keeping eyes on the person. Don’t let strangers touch your clothing to ‘clean’ spills — step back and handle it yourself. Keep valuables in zipped front pockets, not back pockets or open bags. Travel with a companion who can watch your belongings during any distraction. Be especially alert in parks and gardens where ‘joggers’ have plausible cover. If something feels wrong, loudly say ‘Non!’ and create distance.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Restaurant Racketeering & Minimum Spend (tourist-trap, severity: high). Saint-Tropez restaurants have developed sophisticated systems to extract maximum spending from tourists. Restaurants compile secret databases tracking how much each diner spends and tips. If you don’t spend or tip enough, you’ll be blacklisted and refused a table on your next visit. Some establishments demand €5,000 minimum spending or €1,500 per head just to secure a reservation. Despite service charges already being included, staff aggressively pressure tourists for additional ‘American-style’ tips. In one notorious incident, a waiter chased an Italian customer into the parking lot demanding he return inside to add another €500 to his already €500 tip. The mayor of Saint-Tropez has publicly condemned these practices as ‘racketeering.’ How to avoid: Research restaurant policies and reviews before booking. Ask explicitly about minimum spending requirements upfront. Remember that service charge is already included in France. Choose smaller local establishments over famous beach clubs.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Luxury Watch Theft (robbery, severity: high). Organized crews systematically target tourists wearing watches worth €100,000 and up. The operation is disciplined: spotters identify valuable timepieces on beach terraces and at the port, then signal to thieves who either slip the watch off during a staged jostle or yank it off the wrist before escaping on mopeds with tampered plates. Three separate incidents in Saint-Tropez resulted in €400,000 worth of stolen watches in a single weekend. The thefts have grown more brazen, and some have turned violent. How to avoid: Leave valuable watches worth over €5,000 at home. If wearing expensive watches, keep them covered. Stay aware of your surroundings, especially near beach areas. Report suspicious behavior to police immediately.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Villa Rental Fraud (online-fraud, severity: high). Scammers post attractive listings for luxury villas they do not own, using professional photos stolen from real properties and prices that sit just below the market to hook quick bookings. You wire a deposit, get back a fake Airbnb-style confirmation, and only discover the property doesn’t exist — or has already been rented to someone else — when you land. The fraudulent accounts close as soon as the money clears. How to avoid: Book through established local concierge services or established rental agencies, never direct via a stranger. Reverse-image-search every listing photo before paying a deposit. Do not wire transfer — use a credit card so you can dispute. If the price seems too good for the Riviera in July, it is.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Hotel Room Burglary (theft, severity: high). Professional burglars target luxury hotel rooms, particularly those with terrace access. In one case, two British women lost nearly €1 million in valuables — including 11 Hermès Birkin bags, Patek Philippe watches, and Cartier jewelry — after their five-star hotel room was ransacked within hours of check-in. The thieves came in through the private terrace door and ripped the safe out of the wall. A hotel employee was questioned afterward, suggesting inside involvement. How to avoid: Don’t bring valuables worth more than €5,000. Request upper floor rooms without easy exterior access. Keep valuable items with you when possible. Consider travel insurance that covers theft.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Gas Burglary (Villa Gassing) (burglary, severity: high). Criminals allegedly pump anesthetic gas through air conditioning vents or windows to sedate sleeping occupants before robbing them. Notable victims include F1 driver Jenson Button and TV presenter Richard Hammond. Police estimate 90% of villa raids go unreported. However, medical experts dispute whether such ‘knock-out gas’ actually exists as described. How to avoid: Choose upper floor accommodations. Lock all windows and terrace doors. Don’t sleep with windows open. Consider portable door alarms.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Beach Club Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Beach clubs employ questionable practices. Sun loungers cost €35-50 each, and famous clubs like Nikki Beach require €1,500 minimum spend on weekends during high season. Despite websites stating prices include service charges, staff express dissatisfaction with tip amounts. To get weekend reservations at exclusive clubs like Club 55, guests may need to ‘tip’ waiters in advance. How to avoid: Research prices and minimum spend requirements before visiting. Ask for prices upfront before ordering. Remember service charge is already included. Consider less famous beach clubs.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Boat/Yacht Rental Hidden Fees (overcharging, severity: moderate). Boat rental companies advertise attractive daily rates, then stack hidden costs on top: fuel (Saint-Tropez diesel prices run noticeably higher than other ports), delivery and redelivery fees, mooring fees, and water-sports equipment charges. Captain fees vary wildly — the standard rate is €350, but some operators quote €500 or more without justification. Expect unexpected line items for ‘gourmet lunch’ or compulsory insurance add-ons at settlement. How to avoid: Get complete all-inclusive pricing in writing before booking. Compare total costs including fuel across companies. Ask specifically about all potential additional charges.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Pickpocketing & Distraction Theft (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Professional pickpockets operate in crowded tourist areas during summer. Organized gangs use distraction techniques—one member causes a commotion while others target your valuables. Some teams use the ‘petition/clipboard approach.’ Scooter thieves may grab bags or phones from pedestrians. The Tuesday and Saturday markets at Place des Lices are particularly high-risk. How to avoid: Keep bags zipped and in front of you. Don’t carry bags on your street-side shoulder. Use money belts or hidden pouches. Be extra vigilant in crowded market areas.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Taxi Overcharging (transport, severity: moderate). Unlicensed and some licensed taxi drivers target tourists with inflated fares. Common tactics include claiming the meter is broken, taking long routes, or forcing cash payment. Airport transfers from Nice to Saint-Tropez legitimately cost €240-275 (day) or €265-285 (night), but scammers may quote much higher. How to avoid: Use only official taxis from designated stands. Research standard fares before arrival. Use ride-sharing apps like Uber for tracked journeys. Pre-book airport transfers through hotels.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Jet Ski Rental Damage Scam (fraud, severity: moderate). Some jet ski rental operators run a damage-claim scam on returning customers. After you hand back the jet ski, they point to a scratch or crack they claim you caused and demand hundreds of euros for repairs, sometimes with physical intimidation. Refuse to pay, and they threaten to involve police — where mythical ‘administrative charges’ push the demand even higher. How to avoid: Photograph and video the jet ski from every angle before you push off, with visible date and time stamps in the shots. Keep those files safe. Never surrender your passport as collateral. Read recent reviews of the operator before booking — the scam operators have reputations.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Contactless Card Skimming (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). Thieves use digital skimming devices to steal money from contactless-enabled cards without physical contact. They carry concealed readers that capture card information when held close to your wallet or purse in crowded areas, allowing fraudulent purchases or card cloning. How to avoid: Use RFID-blocking wallets or card sleeves. Keep cards in front pockets or secure inner pockets. Regularly monitor card statements for unauthorized charges. Set up transaction alerts on your banking app.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Fake Charity Petitions (pickpocket, severity: low). Scammers approach tourists with clipboards asking them to sign petitions for fake charities. While you’re distracted reading and signing, an accomplice targets your bag or pockets. Even if no theft occurs, you may be pressured to donate money to a non-existent cause. How to avoid: Politely refuse and keep walking. Never stop to engage with clipboard wielders. Keep your belongings secure if you do stop.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Petition/Deaf Charity Clipboard Scam (pickpocket, severity: high). Teams of scammers approach tourists with clipboards asking if they speak English, then request signatures for a fake ‘deaf charity’ petition. While you’re distracted reading or signing, accomplices pickpocket your bags or pockets. After signing, they demand a donation, pointing to text claiming you agreed to donate. The petition is always in English (a red flag in France) and they use exaggerated sign language to appear hearing-impaired. How to avoid: Never stop for clipboard petitioners. Say ‘Non’ firmly and keep walking. Never sign anything on the street. Keep hands on your belongings when approached.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Friendship Bracelet/String Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: moderate). A vendor grabs your hand and begins wrapping colorful string around your wrist before you can refuse. Within seconds, they’ve tied a difficult-to-remove bracelet and demand €10-20 for the ‘gift.’ They become aggressive if you refuse to pay, and may follow you while creating a scene. Sometimes an accomplice uses the distraction to pickpocket you. How to avoid: Keep hands in pockets when walking through tourist areas. Say ‘Non’ firmly and keep walking. Pull your hand away immediately if they try to grab it. Carry small scissors to cut yourself free if necessary.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Gold Ring Scam (street-scam, severity: moderate). A stranger bends down near you and ‘finds’ a gold ring, then asks if you dropped it. When you say no, they examine it and claim it’s marked ’18K gold’ and must be valuable. They offer to sell it for a fraction of its ‘worth’ or ask for a finder’s fee. The ring is worthless brass. While engaging you, an accomplice may be pickpocketing you. How to avoid: Simply say ‘non’ and walk away. Don’t engage in conversation. Be aware of accomplices nearby. Keep hands on belongings.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Tram/Public Transport Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Pickpockets work the crowded Strasbourg trams, particularly Lines B and C that serve the tourist corridors. They move during rush hours and at boarding and exiting, when the crush gives them cover. Teams use distraction techniques: one person blocks your path or stages a bump while an accomplice lifts from your bag or pocket, then exits just as the doors close. How to avoid: Keep bags in front with hands on them. Don’t keep valuables in back pockets. Be extra vigilant when boarding and exiting. If bumped, immediately check belongings.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Counterfeit Attraction Tickets (fraud, severity: moderate). Unlicensed sellers approach tourists outside popular attractions offering ‘discounted’ tickets for boat tours, cathedral tower climbs, or other experiences. The tickets are fake, already used, or for non-existent tours. The seller disappears before you discover the scam. Some pose as official guides offering ‘special access.’ How to avoid: Buy tickets only from official ticket offices. Book tours through established companies. Be suspicious of ‘special deals’ from strangers. Research official prices beforehand.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Christmas Market Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Strasbourg’s famous Christmas markets attract over 2 million visitors annually, creating ideal conditions for pickpockets. The dense crowds, distracting lights, and hands occupied with food and drinks make tourists easy targets. Professional teams work the markets, using distraction techniques or simply taking advantage of the chaos. Valuable items disappear from bags, pockets, and even hands. How to avoid: Wear cross-body bags in front. Keep zippers secured and hands on bags. Leave valuables at hotel. Be extra vigilant in crowded market lanes. Visit during less crowded morning hours.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Taxi Meter Manipulation (transport, severity: low). Some taxi drivers target tourists unfamiliar with local fares. They may claim the meter is broken and quote inflated prices, take unnecessarily long routes, or select the higher night/weekend tariff during regular hours. From the airport to city center, legitimate fare is approximately €40-50 during the day. How to avoid: Insist on using the meter. Know the approximate fare in advance. Use GPS to follow the route. Consider using Uber or official taxi apps. Get receipt for any disputes.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Fake Police/Document Check Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Criminals pose as plainclothes police, flash fake badges, and say they need to check your wallet for counterfeit currency or verify your ID for ‘border security.’ While inspecting your wallet or documents, they palm cash. Strasbourg’s proximity to the German border lets them invent authority for ‘cross-border checks’ — but real French police do not inspect tourists’ wallets on the street. How to avoid: Ask to see official ID clearly and note badge number. Insist on going to nearest police station before showing documents. Never hand over your wallet to anyone on the street. Call 17 (police) if suspicious.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Restaurant Menu Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Restaurants near the Cathedral and in Petite France run a familiar playbook. The English menu shows higher prices than the French one. Waiters bring expensive bottled water without asking, add items you didn’t order, or charge premium prices for Alsatian specialties. Some push for automatic gratuity despite *service compris* already being included in the French price. How to avoid: Ask for the French menu and compare prices. Request ‘une carafe d’eau’ (tap water) — it’s free. Check bill carefully against what you ordered. Know that service is included in French prices. Walk a few streets from major monuments for better value.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — ATM Skimming (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals attach skimming devices to ATMs that capture card data and PINs. Private ATMs like Euronet charge excessive fees and poor exchange rates. Some offer Dynamic Currency Conversion at terrible rates while making it seem like a benefit. Card trap devices may also be used — your card gets stuck and a ‘helpful’ stranger watches you enter your PIN. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside bank branches only. Cover keypad when entering PIN. Wiggle card slot before inserting. Decline dynamic currency conversion. If card gets stuck, don’t leave — call bank immediately.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Bump and Grab/Distraction Theft (pickpocket, severity: high). A well-dressed person ‘accidentally’ bumps into you, spills something on you, or drops items near your feet. While apologizing profusely and helping clean you up or as you helpfully bend down to assist, an accomplice steals from your bag or pockets. Another variation: someone points out a ‘stain’ on your back to distract you. How to avoid: If spilled on, immediately check belongings and move away. Don’t let strangers touch your clothing. Be suspicious of any unusual contact. Keep bags secured in front of you.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Street Vendor Overcharging (overcharging, severity: low). Unlicensed vendors sell cheap souvenirs, ‘artwork,’ or photos at massively inflated prices. They target tourists at photo spots, offering to take pictures then demanding payment for the ‘service.’ Some sell ‘authentic Alsatian’ items that are actually mass-produced imports. They become aggressive when you refuse to buy or try to negotiate. How to avoid: Buy souvenirs from established shops. Decline offers from street vendors. Never hand your camera/phone to unsolicited helpers. Know that most legitimate vendors have fixed prices displayed.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — String/Bracelet Friendship Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: moderate). Near Basilique Saint-Sernin, a vendor approaches tourists and ties a string or friendship bracelet around your wrist, claiming it is a ‘cadeau’ (gift). Once attached, they aggressively demand payment, often blocking your path until you pay. The bracelet is nearly impossible to remove quickly. How to avoid: Keep hands in pockets when approached. Say ‘Non merci’ firmly and keep walking without stopping. Never let anyone tie anything on your wrist.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Gold Ring Scam (street-scam, severity: moderate). Along the Canal du Midi or in the pedestrian zones of the Old Town, a stranger bends down, ‘finds’ a ring on the ground near you, and insists it’s 18-karat gold. They offer to sell it for ‘gas money.’ While you’re looking at the stamp, an accomplice is working your bag or pockets from behind. The ring is brass worth pennies. How to avoid: Ignore any found jewelry and walk away immediately. Head toward the nearest busy cafe or shop if someone persists. Never engage in conversation about found items.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Fake Petition/Deaf-Mute Charity Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Young people at Place du Capitole and Basilique Saint-Sernin — often pretending to be deaf-mute — approach tourists with clipboards asking for signatures on petitions for fake charities. After you sign, they flip to a ‘mandatory donation’ column showing €10–€20 amounts. While your hands are on the clipboard, an accomplice works your bag from behind. How to avoid: Firmly say ‘No’ and walk away without stopping. Never sign anything on the street. These are organized groups and the money never goes to charity.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Metro and Public Transport Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Pickpockets work Toulouse’s metro and bus network, especially during rush hour when carriages are tightly packed. They operate in groups: one person creates a distraction or presses close, the others slip hands into bags and pockets. Line A between Jean Jaurès and Capitole, and buses serving the Old Town, see the most incidents. How to avoid: Keep valuables in front pockets or secure cross-body bags. Be especially vigilant during boarding and exiting when crowds press together. Use money belts for large amounts of cash.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Gare Matabiau Train Station Theft (theft, severity: high). Thefts and muggings are more common around Toulouse’s central train station, Gare Matabiau, than in other parts of the city. The area between Rue Bayard and Allées Jean Jaurès is particularly risky. Luggage theft and distraction pickpocketing are primary concerns. How to avoid: Stay alert at the station and surrounding streets. Keep luggage close and use locks on bags. Avoid walking alone late at night. Use official taxi stands or pre-booked transport.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Fake Police ID Scam (impersonation, severity: high). A stranger approaches asking you to break a large bill. Moments later, a ‘police officer’ arrives with a story about illegal money exchange and asks to inspect your wallet. You get it back with half your cash missing. Some scammers wear armbands and flash fake badges to look official; real French police never inspect tourists’ wallets on the street. How to avoid: Real officers only ask to see ID removed from the wallet, never the wallet itself. Do not hand over your wallet or phone under any circumstances. Ask to see their *carte de police* and offer to walk to the nearest *commissariat* together — genuine police will agree. If something feels off, dial 17.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Taxi Overcharging and Scams (transport, severity: moderate). Some taxi drivers attempt to overcharge tourists by using nighttime tariffs during the day, taking unnecessarily long routes, or claiming the meter is broken. Unofficial taxis without proper markings may charge exorbitant rates. How to avoid: Use only official taxis with clearly marked ‘TAXI’ signs, visible taximeters, and displayed driver details. Ask for an estimate before starting and confirm the route. Note driver numbers if overcharged.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Restaurant Tourist Trap Menu Scam (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Some restaurants offer cheap set menus displayed outside but present different, more expensive menus once seated. Other tactics include menus without prices, pushing medium or large portions only, and serving bottled water without asking. Some bars present inflated bills and use intimidation. How to avoid: Check prices before ordering and confirm them verbally. Avoid restaurants with menus in many languages. Request the same menu shown outside. Always ask for ‘une carafe d’eau’ (tap water) which is free. Review your bill carefully.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — ATM Skimming and Card Fraud (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals install skimming devices on ATMs that capture card data and PINs. Automated service stations and ATMs in tourist areas are frequently targeted. Some scammers approach ATM users offering to ‘help’ while watching PIN entry or claiming the machine is broken to steal inserted cards. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours. Cover the keypad completely when entering your PIN. Check for loose or unusual attachments on card slots. Never accept help from strangers at ATMs.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Rose Seller Distraction Theft (pickpocket, severity: moderate). A scammer approaches with roses, offering one as a ‘free gift.’ Once you accept or touch it, they refuse to take it back and aggressively demand payment. While distracted by the confrontation, an accomplice quietly pickpockets your wallet, phone, or bag. How to avoid: Never accept items from street vendors. Keep hands in pockets and say ‘Non merci’ firmly without breaking stride. Be aware of anyone positioning behind you during such encounters.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Canal-Side Bicycle Grab Theft (theft, severity: high). Thieves on bicycles target outdoor diners along the Canal du Midi and river quays. They rapidly grab phones, cameras, and bags from tables as they cycle past, making pursuit nearly impossible. The theft happens in seconds, often before victims can react. How to avoid: Sit with your back against walls, facing outward. Never leave phones on tablecloths or table edges. Use wrist straps when filming or photographing. Keep bags on your lap or looped around chair legs.

Scam alert in Toulouse, France — Shell Game / Three-Card Monte (gambling-scam, severity: moderate). A street operator sets up a game with three cups and a ball, shuffling quickly and inviting passersby to bet on finding the ball. The entire crowd including ‘winners’ are planted accomplices. The game uses sleight of hand making it impossible to win. While attention is focused on the game, accomplices pickpocket the crowd. How to avoid: Never stop for street gambling games — they are illegal and always rigged. Walk away immediately if you see a crowd gathered around such games. Keep valuables secured.
